bio.en: Timothy Davis led performance marketing for all of Shopify for two and a half years and, as a consultant, helped companies like Pinterest, LinkedIn, Redfin, and Eventbrite build and scale their performance marketing teams.
bio.zh: Timothy Davis 在 Shopify 全面负责效果营销长达两年半，并以顾问身份帮助 Pinterest、LinkedIn、Redfin、Eventbrite 等公司搭建并做大了效果营销团队。

summary.en: Timothy's core thesis is that paid is for everyone at baseline — at minimum paid search, because it's user-driven — but sequencing and evidence matter. He advises starting with Google Search, then Meta, then video/YouTube, and using your own analytics plus small 'signs of life' tests (e.g., 1% lookalikes built from your existing customers) before scaling spend. Critically, don't pour money into ads until you have product-market fit and can actually convert in that market. For team building, hire a data-literate generalist first (someone who finds signal in the noise), then a creative, then a dedicated data scientist; only add headcount when a 'red days' capacity calculator shows the team is genuinely overloaded, and run an 'ops cadence' spreadsheet to stay accountable. Judge performance with platform-native signals (ad strength, click share) and incrementality/Geo experiments rather than vanity metrics, and prefer multi-touch, time-decay attribution. Agencies are fine to start with, but choose partners who plan your exit and dig deep into keyword granularity, landing pages, and conversion paths.
summary.zh: Timothy 的核心观点是：付费广告对每家公司都该做——至少该做付费搜索，因为它是用户主动驱动的——但顺序和证据很重要。他建议先从 Google 搜索做起，再是 Meta，然后是视频/YouTube，并用你自己的分析数据加上小规模的「生命迹象」测试（比如用现有客户建的 1% 类似受众）来验证，再放大投放。关键是，在达成产品市场契合、且能真正在那个市场转化之前，别往广告里砸钱。搭团队时，先招一个懂数据、能从噪音里找信号的通用型人才，再招创意，再招专职数据科学家；只有当「红色天数」容量计算器显示团队真的超负荷时才加人，并用一张「运营节奏」表格来保持问责。评估效果要看平台原生的信号（广告强度、点击份额）和增量性/地理实验，而不是虚荣指标，归因上偏好多触点、时间衰减。代理公司起步时可以用，但要选会为你的退出做规划、并深入到关键词粒度、落地页和转化路径里的人。

It is a different mindset that the user has when they're on there. So that was an example of where we were able to take those instances, look at their data and say, "They're already finding us here. How can we turn this up a little bit?" And I don't remember the numbers exactly, but it was pretty exponential.
turns.zh: 有。几年前我合作过一家公司叫 Hairstory，还有 IPSY。我知道，很好笑。一个没头发的人在做叫 Hairstory 的公司，但他们从 Google 购物这块表现很好。但我开始咨询他们时，我们看了分析数据，其实发现他们当时从 Meta 和 TikTok 拿到不少人。而 TikTok 当时非常新，他们不知道拿它怎么办。于是我们说：「我们做个小测试。」可以先在 Meta 上放点客户证言。看看怎么样。我们拉兴趣、建漏斗、做再营销，希望能转化。TikTok 当时太新了，就像「我们不知道什么会管用。先用手上现有的试试。」（00:10:47）然后一开始做，我们就注意到：「嘿，从创意角度看这不太对。」我们在 Meta 上用的东西行，放到 TikTok 上就不行。所以你不能总把在一个平台上灵的东西直接套到另一个，因为那是不同的用户体验，用户在上面的心态也不同。这就是一个例子：我们能拿那些情况，看他们的数据，然后说：「他们已经在这儿找到我们了。我们怎么稍微开大一点？」具体数字我不记得了，但增长是指数级的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So the core advice here so far, is look for where people are coming to you from today, and then that gives you a sign of where you should start to think about running paid ads, performance marketing on those platforms.
turns.zh: 好。所以到目前为止的核心建议是：看人们今天从哪来，这就给了你信号——你该从哪些平台开始考虑跑付费广告、做效果营销。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. And also, there's a saying that my current director likes to use, which is signs of life. You can always do a very, very small test. You can just put a little money into a platform, see if there's a sign of life. If there is, then you can pull back and say, "Okay, we have signs of life. Now let's build a campaign around that." There's no reason to say, "All right, we have a signs of life. Let's now turn it up all the way." Do we have the right creative? Do we have the right campaign? Do we have the right messaging for the users on this platform? Then let's take that approach, as opposed to just, "Hey, signs of life, great, go run a hundred miles an hour." Make sure you're doing the right thing when you get into those platforms.
turns.zh: 对。另外，我现在那个总监喜欢用一句话，叫「生命迹象」。你永远可以做个非常小非常小的测试。往一个平台里放一点钱，看有没有生命迹象。如果有，你就可以退回来想：「好，我们有生命迹象了。现在围绕它建一个 campaign。」没理由说「好，有生命迹象了，那我们直接开到一百迈」。我们有没有对的创意？有没有对的 campaign？有没有对这个平台用户对的 messaging？然后再采取那个方式，而不是「嘿，有生命迹象，太好了，直接全速跑」。进这些平台时，要确保你做的是对的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's follow that thread. A lot of people run little experiments on say, TikTok, and Snap, and Twitter, and things like LinkedIn, and they often don't see a lot of results and it's always like, "Hey, did we do it wrong or is it the platform's not working?" I know it's a very difficult question to give like, "Here's how you do a sign of life test correctly," But what are some things that you think either people do often wrong when they're trying to experiment with the platform or that you just think they should do when they're trying to look for signs of life?
turns.zh: 顺着这个线。很多人在 TikTok、Snap、Twitter，还有 LinkedIn 这类地方跑小实验，常常看不到什么结果，然后总说「是我们做错了，还是这平台本来就不行？」我知道要给出「怎么正确做生命迹象测试」很难，但你觉得人们试平台时常做错什么，或者你觉得他们在找生命迹象时应该做什么？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: The number one thing I tell people all the time is use your own data, start with your own data. So take the existing customer base you have, load that up into the platform to build lookalikes. From there, you can do... And I'll use Meta as the example. You can do a 1%, all the way up to a 10%. So 1% match, 2%, 3%, so on and so forth. (00:13:12): What I tend to do is build ad sets, one at 1% because we know that one's going to be highly correlated to what we're looking for. Then a two to four, and then a five to seven, and then an eight plus. More times than not, the eight plus does not work, but there have been times where it has, so it's, "Hey, let's do it. Let's try it." But if you also have a very limited budget because some people don't have the luxury of having an unlimited budget like we do in some of these other companies I've worked at, just start with the 1%. See what that sign of life is because you already know that this is so tied to your existing customer base. If that sign of life is giving you a positive signal, now you have the information you need to build a campaign you need to be successful.
turns.zh: 我一直在跟人说的第一件事，是用你自己的数据，从你自己的数据开始。把你现有的客户群体弄上去，加载进平台去建类似受众。从那出发，你能做……我用 Meta 当例子。你可以做 1%，一直到 10%。1% 匹配、2%、3%，以此类推。（00:13:12）我通常的做法是建广告组，一个在 1%，因为我们知道那个跟我们要找的人高度相关。然后是 2 到 4，再是 5 到 7，再是 8 以上。多数时候 8 以上的不行，但也有行的时候，所以就「嘿，做吧，试试。」但如果你预算非常有限——有些人没我待过的那些公司那种无限预算的奢侈——就从 1% 开始。看那个生命迹象是什么，因为你知道这跟你现有客户群绑定得多紧。如果那个生命迹象给了你正面信号，你就有了建一个能成功的 campaign 所需的信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are these percentages referring to? You may have mentioned it, but when you say 1%, 2%, 3%.
turns.zh: 你说的这些百分比指什么？你可能提过，但你说 1%、2%、3% 的时候——

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So that is how closely tied they are to that user's behavior on the platform. So they're 1% tied to what they're doing. They're visiting similar pages or they have similar behavior on the platform, so they're more than likely going to be tied to what that user... They're not going to be that user exactly, but they're going to be very correlated to them where 10% is pretty wide base that you're going to hit.
turns.zh: 对，对。那是说他们跟那个用户在平台上的行为绑得多紧。1% 是跟他们在做的事高度相关——他们访问类似的页面、在平台上有类似行为，所以他们极可能跟那个用户相关——不一定是那个用户本人，但非常相关；而 10% 是个很宽的基础，你会打到一大片。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So the smaller the percentage, the closer they are, the closer it will look like there.
turns.zh: 我懂了。所以百分比越小，他们越接近，看起来越像那群人。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yep, there you go.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you know if it's the creative that is failing versus it's just never going to work? Is there something that tells you that's what's not working?
turns.zh: 你怎么知道是创意在失败，还是它本来就不行？有没有什么能告诉你「这不工作」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: It's a million-dollar question, to be honest with you. Because you could look at some of the metrics that currently exist in the platform. Click-through rate basically just tells you, are the users engaged? Because start with the target. You're getting the impressions are there. Is the target right? That should be your first thing. Yes, the target is correct. Users that we want to see are seeing our ads, but they're not engaging with it. That would be the first thing. (00:15:15): But the part that I think you're really trying to ask is creative versus the content. Because sometimes depending on the ad unit, you could have a story creative that is literally the creative has to stand on its own, not necessarily the content that's in it, but something like an in-feed creative has a headline, a primary, a description, and a creative. That's where honestly, the only way you're going to get an answer to that outside of the data that's available to you like click-through rate, reach, frequency and all those things to pull in more metrics, is a focus group to understand, "Hey, when you saw this image with this content, what was your result from it?" (00:15:58): Now, you can build a test within the platform to do a control versus a test where say, you take the creative with the same primary and the same description versus a creative that's just your logo with the headline and the description and see what the results are. But more times than not, you're not getting the understanding from the user of, well, why doesn't that creative resonate with you? And they'll give you suggestions in the focus group. Why does that work better for you than not? So that's a really, really hard question to answer without having those dialogue with the user to understand that.
turns.zh: 说实话，这是个百万美元的问题。因为你可以看平台里现有的一些指标。点击率基本只告诉你：用户有没有参与？因为先从目标看。曝光有了。目标对吗？那该是你第一件事。对，目标是对的，想看我们广告的人看到了，但他们没参与。那是第一点。（00:15:15）但我觉得你真正想问的是创意和内容。因为有时看广告单元，你可能有个 story 创意，创意得自己立得住，不一定是里面的内容；但像信息流里的创意，有标题、主文案、描述，还有创意本身。说实话，除了平台里可用的数据——点击率、覆盖、频次这些——去拉更多指标，唯一能让你得到答案的，是焦点小组，去理解「嘿，当你看到这张图配这个内容，你得到的是什么结果？」（00:15:58）现在你可以在平台里建一个对照测试，比如拿「同样主文案、同样描述、但创意换成只有 logo 配标题描述」对比「原创意」，看结果如何。但多数时候，你无法从用户那儿得到「为什么那个创意不引起共鸣」的理解——焦点小组里他们会给你建议，为什么那个对你更好。所以没有跟用户对话去理解，这个问题真的很难答。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. How long do you recommend these tests run for these signs of life tests? And I like this term, by the way. I haven't heard this before.
turns.zh: 对，很有道理。你建议这些生命迹象测试跑多久？顺便说，我喜欢「生命迹象」这个词，之前没听过。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Ideally, in a perfect world, you're going to hear the word, statistical relevance. Mathematicians will tell you exactly what that number is. And I'm not going to pretend like a mathematician, but a lot of times, it's budget constraint. So there could be a VP finance. Anyone like that could just come to you and just say, "Hey, do you have $25,000 for this test?" You only have 5,000. Just get that information, get that data. You can then also build an off size off of that. Hey guys, we worked with our Meta partners, we worked with our Google partners. We put $1,000 behind this test. We know that our impression share was this, our reach was this. If we were to put $10,000 into it, this is the expected return we can get from it based on the click-through rate, the conversion rate that we got from the test that we ran.
turns.zh: 理想情况下，完美的世界里你会听到「统计显著性」这个词。数学家会告诉你那个数字确切是多少。我不想假装是数学家，但很多时候是预算限制。可能有个财务 VP 之类的人来跟你说：「嘿，这测试你有 2.5 万刀吗？」你只有 5 千。就拿到那个信息、那个数据。你也能据此建一个推算。嘿各位，我们跟 Meta 的合作伙伴、Google 的合作伙伴合作，在这个测试上放了 1000 刀。我们知道我们的曝光份额是这些、覆盖是这些。如果我们投 1 万进去，基于我们跑的测试拿到的点击率和转化率，这是预期的回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So basically, we have limited number of dollars to spend. That'll tell you how long you could run one of these for.
turns.zh: 懂了。所以基本上，我们能花的钱有限，那就告诉你能把一个测试跑多久。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other tips for someone that's trying to experiment with a platform early on for these signs of life tests? So one is try a lookalike that is the most targeted version of the lookalike. So 1% you said, and then incrementally grown and incrementally increase that percentage as you spend more. Any other tips, I guess, for people just to experiment with the platform?
turns.zh: 对刚开始在平台上做生命迹象测试的人，还有别的建议吗？一个是试最精准版本的类似受众，就是你说 1%，然后随着花得更多逐步放大那个百分比。我猜对试平台的人还有别的建议？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Make sure you're not too hard on yourself if it doesn't work. A lot of times, companies I've either consulted with or worked at, there was always pressure or there was always a need to succeed at whatever experiment we put into market. I believe in creating an environment where it's okay to fail because we're either winning or we're learning. And more times than not, if we put something new into a platform that we know nothing about, we're learning the bells and whistles, we're learning the functionality of it. Just know there's going to be things you're not going to understand because each platform is unique, each platform is different, the user behavior is different. So give yourself some grace, understand that this may not work. And as long as you're learning from it, you're going to be okay.
turns.zh: 要是没成，别对自己太狠。很多时候，我咨询过或待过的公司，总有一种压力、一种必须让每个放出去的实验成功的需求。我信奉营造一种「失败没关系」的环境，因为我们要么赢、要么学到。多数时候，如果我们把一个全新、一无所知的平台里放了新东西，我们是在学它的门道、学它的功能。要知道会有你不理解的东西，因为每个平台独特、不同，用户行为不同。所以给自己点宽容，明白这可能不行。只要你能从中学习，就没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. In terms of which platforms people should explore, obviously there's Google, there's Facebook, Instagram, what are the platforms people should seriously consider at this point?
turns.zh: 我喜欢。关于该探索哪些平台，显然有 Google、Facebook、Instagram，现在大家该认真考虑哪些平台？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Google for sure. And when we say Google, let's make sure everyone understands what Google entails. Google is YouTube, Google is Google search, GDN, Google Display Network. There's a lot of things in Google that you can do. I always say, if you have the creative available, you should really, really be looking at doing video because video is one of those things that I'm very bullish on. It is doing really well when you measure it the right way. And as long as you can get that creative and get it consistently just because you have one piece of creative, if it's doing well, you do need to have that creative refresh, kind of that flywheel going. Make sure you're doing Google Search, again, user-driven, YouTube, and Meta, and Meta contains both Facebook and Instagram. And then based on the data available to you, if you do see users on TikTok, definitely go after those. But if you're just starting out and you just want to get your feet wet into something, I would say start with Google Search, then get into Meta. And if you have video available, definitely get into YouTube.
turns.zh: Google 肯定。我们说 Google 时，要确保大家都理解 Google 包含什么。Google 有 YouTube、有 Google 搜索、有 GDN（Google 展示广告网络）。Google 里你能做的事很多。我总说，如果你有可用的创意，真的应该认真看视频，因为视频是我非常看好的。只要用对方式衡量，它表现很好。而且只要你能量产创意——因为就算你只有一条创意、它表现好，你确实得有创意的刷新，形成那种飞轮。一定要做 Google 搜索（再次强调，用户驱动的）、YouTube，还有 Meta（Meta 包含 Facebook 和 Instagram）。然后基于你可用的数据，如果你确实看到用户在 TikTok 上，绝对去追。但如果你刚开始、只想先沾点水，我会说从 Google 搜索开始，再进 Meta。如果你有视频，绝对进 YouTube。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. So Google Search, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok. What about LinkedIn? Do you see things happening there for say, B2B companies?
turns.zh: 好。所以 Google 搜索、YouTube、Facebook、Instagram、TikTok。那 LinkedIn 呢？你看 B2B 公司在那儿有动静吗？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. LinkedIn is very expensive in comparison. So just know if you're going into LinkedIn, it's going to look almost three times more expensive than other channels. The targeting that's available on LinkedIn, knowing job titles, industries, actually targeting people at certain companies is very powerful. The example I always tend to use is that I worked at a company called SoftLayer. SoftLayer was acquired by IBM because they were trying to build out their cloud portfolio, couldn't do it. So they're like, "Hey, let's do the next best thing and buy this company." But when we were just SoftLayer, we were trying to get Coca-Cola as one of our clients. And you know those Coke freestyles where you can pick whatever drink you want and put the flavor in it?
turns.zh: 对。LinkedIn 相对贵很多。所以要知道，进 LinkedIn 看起来差不多是其他渠道的三倍贵。但 LinkedIn 上可用的定向——知道职位、行业，直接定向某些公司的人——非常强。我总用的例子是我在一家叫 SoftLayer 的公司。SoftLayer 被 IBM 收购了，因为他们想建自己的云产品组合、建不成，于是说「嘿，做下一个最好的事，买下这家公司」。但我们还只是 SoftLayer 的时候，想拿下可口可乐当客户。你知道那些 Coke Freestyle 机器吗，你能选任何饮料、加口味？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, that's awesome.
turns.zh: 不知道，那个超赞。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Oh man, these are great. Maybe it's a cell thing, but basically, you go up to a Coke freestyle and say, "I want Dr. Pepper and I want cherry flavor in it." Or you want Coke Zero with cherry and vanilla in it, you can do that. It's the freestyle you get to pick. The reason they wanted it to be cloud-based is because there's a ton of drinks in there. So you need to be able to efficiently and effectively say, "This store needs more Sprite or this store needs more Sprite Zero." Because you have your whole portfolio in this one machine, so you want to be able to update things more readily. And it was between us, AWS and Microsoft. And met with the sales team and said, "What do we need to do to win this?" Because it was a big ticket item for us. (00:22:14): And what we found out was they had two concerns about us. It was recency and private security. So what we did was we found out where the decision makers were. So A, in LinkedIn, we took the anyone who works at Coca-Cola, we want you to see ads about security and recency. Outside of that, we also geo-fenced it because you would think Coca-Cola Atlanta, that's where the decision maker sits, but they were actually in LA. So in LA, we geo-fenced them, and we knew that they worked at Coca-Cola. The next time the salesperson got on the call with the team to say, "Hey, just wanted to check in." He was like, "Hey, hey, I get it. Security is fine. Recency is fine. We hear you." That was great to hear because it was something we were able to do on LinkedIn and we did it in other platforms as well. But we knew we were able to get not only to the decision maker, but everyone around that decision maker to say, "Hey, these guys may be the ones we need to go with."
turns.zh: 哦天，那些超棒。可能是便利店里的东西，但 basically 你走到一台 Coke Freestyle 前说「我要 Dr. Pepper 加樱桃味」，或者 Coke Zero 加樱桃和香草味，都能行。那是 freestyle，你随便挑。他们想让它云端化，是因为机器里饮料太多了，你需要高效地说「这家店需要更多 Sprite，那家店需要更多 Sprite Zero」。因为你整个产品组合都在这台机器里，你想能更即时地更新。当时是我们、AWS 和微软三家在争。我们跟销售团队碰了，问「要赢这个，我们得做什么？」因为对我们是个大单。（00:22:14）我们发现他们对我们有两个顾虑：时效性和私有安全。于是我们找到了决策者在哪里。首先，在 LinkedIn 上，我们定向所有在可口可乐工作的人，让他们看到关于安全和时效性的广告。除此之外我们还做了地理围栏，因为你以为可口可乐决策者在亚特兰大总部，但其实他们在 LA。所以在 LA 我们对他们做了地理围栏，而且我们知道他们在可口可乐工作。下次销售跟那团队打电话说「嘿，只是想跟进一下」，对方说「嘿，嘿，我懂。安全没问题，时效性也没问题。我们听到了。」听到这个太好了，因为那是我们在 LinkedIn 上能做到、也在别的平台做了的。但我们能同时触达决策者、以及决策者周围所有人，让他们说「嘿，这几个人可能就是我们要选的。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So just to mirror back what you're saying, you're saying you ran ads on LinkedIn targeting the execs at Coca-Cola, trying to influence them to overcome these barriers they had to buying to working with you guys. Amazing. I've seen people do that on Google Search, but I've never heard of... It makes so much sense to do on LinkedIn and it worked. And did they know that you did this or they're just like, "Oh, I just changed my mind"?
turns.zh: 好。我复述一下你说的：你在 LinkedIn 上跑了广告，定向可口可乐的高管，想影响他们克服买我们东西的障碍。太妙了。我在 Google 搜索上见过人这么干，但从没听说过……在 LinkedIn 上做这么合理、而且成了。他们知道你这么干了吗，还是就「哦，我自己改了主意」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: One of them was like, "We get it. We're seeing it everywhere." We actually tried because at the time, we didn't have an offline team. We actually tried to buy the billboards around the office as well, but I didn't know enough at the time from an offline perspective of the right people to talk to, how long it would take to do it. So we were trying to pour it on hard.
turns.zh: 其中一个说「我们懂。我们到处都看到了。」我们其实试过，因为当时我们没有线下团队。我们其实也想把办公室周围的广告牌买下来，但我当时对线下不够懂——该找谁谈、要花多久。所以我们是想全力压上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's incredible. I could see why LinkedIn is more expensive. That's incredibly powerful. And is the advice then that LinkedIn makes more sense for higher LTV, higher CB type of products?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。我能理解为什么 LinkedIn 更贵。这威力太大了。那你的建议是 LinkedIn 更适合高 LTV、高客单价这类产品？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I would not recommend getting into LinkedIn and my LinkedIn reps may kill me for this. I would not recommend getting into LinkedIn until you've tested Google and Meta first. Now, you could be an enterprise level company and it does make sense to start with LinkedIn for sure, but depending on your audience, I would say more times than not, it would be a Google, Meta discussion before going to LinkedIn.
turns.zh: 对，没错。我不会推荐一上来就进 LinkedIn——我的 LinkedIn 销售代表可能会杀了我。我不会推荐在测过 Google 和 Meta 之前进 LinkedIn。当然，如果你是个企业级公司，从 LinkedIn 开始确实合理，但看你的受众，我会说多数情况是先聊 Google、Meta，再去 LinkedIn。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So just generally, start with Google and Meta. Is there one or the other usually? I guess, yeah, which one would you start with if you had to pick one?
turns.zh: 好。所以一般先从 Google 和 Meta 开始。有哪个优先吗？如果只能选一个，你先从哪个开始？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Always Google Search. I'm always going to say, start with Google search, but it's also creative dependent. If you don't have the right creative for Facebook, it's going to be really hard to convert because users are just going to either be turned off by what you're putting out there. And then also, depending on where your user base is. If they're not on Facebook, it's kind of a moot point. But if they're browsing around on GDN or YouTube, it makes more sense to go there.
turns.zh: 永远 Google 搜索。我永远会说从 Google 搜索开始，但这也看创意。如果你没有对的 Facebook 创意，会很难转化，因为用户会被你放出去的东西劝退。而且看你的用户群在哪。如果他们不在 Facebook，那也没意义。但如果他们在 GDN 或 YouTube 上逛，去那儿更合理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you said this insight about video is performing super well right now and you're recommending people use video. And the key there is you need to be able to make videos, video ads.
turns.zh: 然后你提到视频现在表现特别好，你推荐大家用视频。关键是你得能制作视频、视频广告。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. You got to make sure you have that flywheel.
turns.zh: 对。你得确保你有那个飞轮。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the flywheel is just people internally or some company agency that can make video ads for you?
turns.zh: 飞轮就是内部有人、或者某家公司/代理能帮你做视频广告？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Correct. Yep.
turns.zh: 对。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. I guess, is there any advice there of just how to do that or what ads work well or anything there for someone else-
turns.zh: 酷。那这方面有什么建议吗，怎么做，或者什么广告效果好，给别人——

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: So yeah. The thing with YouTube is I always say, start with emotion. If you can have an emotional connection with the user, is going to be way more impactful and way more powerful than anything else. And to take that further, when I say emotion, I'm talking about comedy, I'm talking about...
turns.zh: 对。YouTube 这事我总说，从情绪开始。如果你能跟用户建立情感连接，会比别的一切都有力、都强。再进一步说，我说情绪，是指喜剧、是指……

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: I'm talking about happiness. It's not necessarily just, "Oh, we need an emotional connection with the brand." It is just making sure the user feels something after seeing your ad. Because then, they're more times not going to remember it, which then they will take a favorable action after the fact.
turns.zh: 是指快乐。不一定要「哦，我们要跟品牌建立情感连接」。就是确保用户看了你的广告后有所感觉。因为那样，他们多数时候会记住它，之后会采取有利的行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super interesting. One last question about platforms. Are there any other platforms you see working for people that are emerging maybe that people aren't thinking about, Reddit, or Snap, or X, or I don't know, anything along those lines?
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。关于平台最后一个问题。还有没有别的新兴平台你觉得在起作用、大家没在想的，比如 Reddit、Snap、X，或者这类？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: When you say emerging channels, my brain kind of goes to connected TV, podcast, VR, advertising, audio/voice search, and even AI stuff right now. I can tell you podcasts are doing really well for the people that I know are able to measure it correctly. Connected TV is also doing really well. You can take the, again, you're doing YouTube right now, being able to take that creative and repurpose it. But the VR stuff and the AI stuff, that is stuff that is, I would say, very emerging right now. Because to be completely transparent, I haven't experimented with those things yet. I kind of like letting other people be the guinea pig and learning from them, and then if someone comes to me and they're like, "Hey, we have budget for this, let's go ahead and test it." "Great. Let's go. Let's see what we can learn."
turns.zh: 你说新兴渠道，我脑子会转到联网电视、播客、VR 广告、语音搜索，甚至现在的 AI 东西。我能告诉你，播客对我认识、且能正确衡量的人表现很好。联网电视也很好。你已经在做 YouTube 了，能把那创意拿去复用。但 VR 和 AI 那些，我说现在非常新兴。因为坦白讲，我还没试过那些。我有点喜欢让别人当小白鼠、从他们那学，然后如果有人来找我说「嘿，我们有预算，去测这个」，「好，走，看看能学到什么。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Podcast ads. I'm glad you suggested that. I'm a huge fan. Thank you. They're working really well for a lot of our sponsors and I'm very biased, so you don't need to pay attention to me. But I also think there's a lot of opportunity there. Okay. Let's talk about when to start investing in performance marketing/paid growth. So, say, you're a startup, do you have any advice for when it's time to start, signs of life test or even... And then also, just when is it time to scale to go like, "Okay, let's go big on this."
turns.zh: 好。播客广告。很高兴你提了。我是大粉丝。谢谢。对我们很多赞助商都很好用，而且我有偏见，所以你不用理我。但我也觉得那里机会很大。好，聊聊什么时候开始投效果营销/付费增长。比如你是个初创公司，什么时候开始、做生命迹象测试，或者什么时候该放大、说「好，我们在这上面下重注」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: If you are a startup, typically, whenever I consulted with them, it was what are the goals, what are we trying to achieve, and when? Because if you're looking for something quick, paid needs to start immediate. And paid [inaudible 00:28:24] started yesterday because SEO takes time. SEO, depending on the market you're getting into, if it's emerging, people may not even know your product exists. There was a product I was working on years ago that if you were traveling to a hotel, and say, it was a romantic getaway with you and your partner. And you wanted the hotel suite or room done up with flower petals, and champagne, and stuff like that, they would do it for you. Well, they were working with someone before that was like, "Oh, we should totally be in paid search." And if you look at the keywords that they were doing, it was like, booking hotel rooms. It's like, "No, that's complete disconnect." And they're like, "Yeah, but we're trying to build awareness." (00:29:08): You don't want to build awareness through search. You build awareness through display media-based type media. When we transitioned all of their money over at the time, and this will age me, before Meta was a thing, when we transitioned everything over to GDN, that's when the company started really reaping the rewards. Because we were building the awareness around the product. So, it depends on what is the demand of your product and market. If you're doing something that is similar to another product and market, you could do competitor, I call it coattail riding. Say, Lenny, you and I create a product that is similar to monday.com. We can go out there and just start bidding on monday.com and say, "See why Lenny and Tim are better than monday.com." And start getting some people in interested, maybe kicking the tires, starting free trials, but they also have other keywords that they can go after in market. But if you're going after something new like hotel room, flowers, and I forget what keywords we were bidding on for that, it was years ago. People weren't thinking of that. It wasn't something they were searching for. So, it just really depends on, A, when do you expect results because SEO can take time. And B, what is the demand in the market for your product?
turns.zh: 如果你是初创公司，通常我咨询时，会问目标是什么、我们想达成什么、什么时候。因为如果你要快的东西，付费得立刻开始。付费[听不清]昨天就该开始了，因为 SEO 要时间。SEO 看你要进的市场，如果是新兴的，人家可能根本不知道你的产品存在。多年前我做过一个产品，如果你去酒店度假、和你伴侣的浪漫之旅，你想让套房或房间用花瓣、香槟布置好，他们会帮你做。之前合作的人说「哦，我们该做付费搜索」。你看他们用的关键词，是「订酒店房间」。我说「不，那完全不搭。」他们说「但我们想建认知。」（00:29:08）你不该通过搜索建认知，你通过展示类媒体建认知。当我们把他们的钱全转过去——这显老了我，在 Meta 出现之前——转去 GDN 时，公司才开始真正收获回报。因为我们在建产品的认知。所以这取决于你产品的需求和市场的需求。如果你做的东西和另一个产品、市场类似，你可以做竞品，我叫「搭顺风车」。比如 Lenny，你和我做个类似 monday.com 的产品。我们可以出去对 monday.com 出价，说「看看为什么 Lenny 和 Tim 比 monday.com 好」，吸引一些人感兴趣、试试、开免费试用，但他们也有别的在市关键词可以追。但如果你做的是像酒店房间、花这种新东西，我忘了关键……[截断]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Some people use paid ads to drive early growth to bring customers, to help them figure out what to build kind of pre-product market fit growth. Is that something you recommend? Is that something you'd advise against? Is that strategy that you've seen work?
turns.zh: 有些人用付费广告驱动早期增长、拉客户，帮他们搞清楚该建什么——有点产品市场契合前的增长。你推荐这个吗？你会反对吗？你见过这种策略成功吗？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. Product market fit is a huge thing. We've run into some of this at Shopify, and we definitely ran into this at IBM. So, for the longest time, IBM is, "We're a global company, we should be everywhere." But when we started looking at the data, it was, "Should we be everywhere?" For example, Africa, we were in the whole continent. We weren't just in, say, South Africa, or Egypt, or something like that. And the more we dug into it, the more we realized the biggest issue wasn't necessarily that users weren't interested in our product and weren't purchasing it, it was because we didn't have a product market fit mainly from an operation standpoint. (00:31:33): In Africa, there are multitudes of different types of currency. There's the franc, there's the rand, there's the shill, and we were just, "Hey, USD, thank you." So, of course, they weren't converting unless they were going out of their way to make a way to convert that. So, when we took a step back and we said, "Okay, where do we want to start?" It was South Africa. That's really where we were trying to get, quote, unquote, "stronghold" in, so we had to make sure we had the rand available. Once we did that, we started doing tremendously better because we had a product market fit. They had demand for our product, and now we were able to serve them, meet them where they were.
turns.zh: 对。产品市场契合是大事。我们在 Shopify 碰过这个，在 IBM 肯定也碰过。很长一段时间，IBM 是「我们是全球公司，我们该无处不在」。但我们看数据时，是「我们该无处不在吗？」比如非洲，我们整个大陆都进了，不只是南非或埃及之类。我们越挖越发现，最大问题不一定是用户对产品不感兴趣、不买，而是我们从运营角度没有产品市场契合。（00:31:33）在非洲，有各种货币，有法郎、兰特、先令，我们却只说「嘿，美元，谢了」。所以当然，除非他们特意想办法去换，否则不转化。于是我们退一步说「好，我们从哪开始？」是南非。那才是我们想拿下的「据点」，所以我们得确保有兰特可用。一旦做了，我们表现好太多了，因为我们有了产品市场契合。他们有需求，现在我们能服务他们、在他们所在的地方接住他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So essentially, you're saying probably not smart to run a bunch of ads if it's not working, if you don't have something people actually want yet in that market?
turns.zh: 所以本质上你是说，如果在一个市场里东西不行、人们其实还不想买，跑一堆广告大概不聪明？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Right. Or able to convert.
turns.zh: 对。或者没法转化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because conversion is going to end up being really low, no one actually cares about what you're doing.
turns.zh: 因为转化率最终会很低，根本没人在乎你在干嘛。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: All you're going to do is really annoy the users. Because, say, in the future they are, "Hey, I'm still interested, but I don't want to use that product because I already tried." It's like, "No, no, you can totally use it now." "I already tried. I had a bad experience with them." And some users will hold you accountable to that. One bad experience and I'm just never giving you my business.
turns.zh: 你只会真的惹恼用户。因为假设将来他们说「嘿，我还有兴趣，但我不想用那产品，因为我试过了」。就像「不不，你现在完全能用」。「我已经试过了。体验很差。」有些用户会为此追究你。一次坏体验，我就永远不给你生意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So, is that generally your advice if you're startup, you're not feeling like you actually have product market fit yet, should you even experiment with and do signs of life tests, or should you hold off until it's like, "Okay, it's actually working, let's go."
turns.zh: 有意思。那一般来说，如果你初创、觉得自己还没真正有产品市场契合，你该试生命迹象测试吗，还是该等到「好，它真的行了，我们上」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: From an operation standpoint, I always want to make sure those things are tied off. Yeah, it doesn't make sense to, again, if you have a major budget and you're trying to get awareness into a market, great, yeah, you can go after a market. But just know that it's probably not going to convert very well.
turns.zh: 从运营角度，我永远想确保那些事都收尾了。对，如果你有大预算、想对一个市场建认知，那去追那个市场没问题。但要知道它可能转化不会太好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So-
turns.zh: 懂了。所以——

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: I wouldn't recommend it.
turns.zh: 我不推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. Awesome. Very clear answer. Let's talk about the mistakes that you see companies make when they're investing in performance marketing. We got introduced through Casey Winters's illustrious former podcast guest, two-time podcast guest and asked them about you. And he told me that when you take over for an agency at a company that you've worked with, you crush their performance within a month. I'm curious to what you see and find they are doing wrong that allows you to be such a hero when you come in and take over.
turns.zh: 好，很棒。非常清楚的回答。聊聊你看到公司在投效果营销时常犯的错。我们是通过 Casey Winters 那档有名的播客介绍的，他两次上节目，我问他要了你。他告诉我，你接手一家公司的代理公司时，一个月内就把他们的效果碾压了。我好奇你看到、发现他们做错了什么，让你进来接手时能当英雄。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: I think agencies have playbooks. Now I've worked at agencies, I did consulting for a long period of time and it was never an approach I took. I looked at each account and each company as its own thing. But I think a lot of agencies just come in and they go, "Oh, this is like AB&C company. And this is what we're doing. Copy, paste, done, move on." And they're also not willing to get deep, deep, deep into the weeds of stuff. I may get a little too far into data than some other people. For example, I have ops cadence that myself and my team follow. So, within that ops cadence, we have things like finance, performance, structure, keywords, ad copy, quality score, targeting, et cetera, et cetera. And then, within each of those we have specifics. For example, the keyword subsection is keyword granularity, brand versus non-brand, search query reports, negative, so on so forth. (00:35:06): I feel like agencies don't necessarily get into all of those things every single month where some of those we're doing weekly, some of those we're doing biweekly, and some of those we're doing monthly. But they touch the things that they think they need to touch. They turn on automated bidding, they're doing their search query reports, and then they just kind of move on with their day because they have 50 other clients they have to get to. Well, what about looking at your conversions? Where are we converting? Have we tested different landing pages? What is a better user experience that we could be getting users right now? It's a five-step process, can we get it to a three? Partnering with PMMs to say, "Hey, here's something that I think could help improve our lead to conversion." Just stuff like that, that they're too busy with too many other things to focus really, really deep into those. (00:36:03): And typically, whenever I managed an agency in the past and I consulted, I made sure that you weren't stretched thin enough that you couldn't do those things. Because I'm a firm believer in hiring smart people and then getting out of their way. But each week having one-on-ones with them, just spot checking things, just saying, "Hey, I looked at this. This doesn't look right. What's going on there?" "Oh yeah, I do that on this day." "Okay, great. Just making sure you're covered." Because sometimes people won't scream uncle when they should be screaming uncle because they think it's a sign of weakness. (00:36:40): But let me know when you're overwhelmed. Maybe I have a solution for you. Maybe there's a way I can coach you to be better at something, or we just need to hire more resources. Because the client portfolio you have is five, and when we took them on, they were all at 100K, but now they're all spending 2 million plus. We need to offload some of that from you because you're doing such a good job that you've scaled them up. Let's give you three clients instead of five and hire someone to take those two.
turns.zh: 我觉得代理公司有套路。我也在代理公司干过，咨询做了很长时间，那从来不是我的方式。我把每个账户、每家公司当成独立的东西看。但很多代理公司进来就说「哦，这跟 A、B、C 公司一样。就这么做。复制、粘贴、完事、下一个。」而且他们也不愿意钻到那些细节的最深处。我可能会比一些人钻数据钻得更深。比如我有个运营节奏，我和团队都遵守。在那个节奏里，我们有财务、效果、结构、关键词、广告文案、质量得分、定向等等。然后在每个下面还有具体的。比如关键词那块，有关键词粒度、品牌词 vs 非品牌词、搜索词报告、否定词等等。（00:35:06）我觉得代理公司不一定要每个月都碰所有这些，而我们有些每周做、有些双周、有些每月。但他们只碰他们认为该碰的。他们打开自动出价，做搜索词报告，然后一天就过了，因为他们还有 50 个其他客户要顾。那看转化呢？我们在哪转化？我们测过不同落地页吗？现在能给用户更好的体验是什么？是个五步流程，能压成三步吗？跟产品经理合作说「嘿，我觉得这能让潜客到转化的效率更高」？就是这类事，他们太忙、顾太多别的事，没法真正钻深。（00:36:03）通常我以前管代理、做咨询时，会确保他们不会被拉得太薄、以至于做不了这些。因为我坚信……[截断]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it sounds like basically they just don't have the time to care and spend on all the things that they need to be doing. And when you've held companies, you actually go deep and you have the time to do it well. I guess, when someone's trying to find an agency or someone like you, I know you don't do this much anymore. Any advice for just how to know if they're going to be great? Is it just agencies in general probably not a good choice? Is it hire someone in-house? I guess, what advice do you offer people that are like, "Oh man, I want to avoid this."
turns.zh: 所以听起来基本上是他们没时间关心、没时间投入该做的所有事。而你接手公司时，你是真钻进去、有时间做好。我猜当一个人想找代理或像你这样的人——我知道你现在不大做这个了——有什么建议能判断他们会不会很棒？是代理整体可能都不是好选择？还是招个内部的人？对想「哦天，我想避开这个」的人，你给什么建议？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Agencies are a good place to get things started. Even when I was consulting, I would, honestly, I'm a big believer in forward thinking, backwards planning. So, if I'm taking this contract on with this new client, what's the end goal for you? If your end goal is to have this at performing in $100 million spend, there's no way one person can do that. So let's create milestones along the way of making sure we're checking in and saying, when is the right time to hire? Whether that's a data scientist, whether that's a creative person in-house or replacing me full time. There's no reason that you should be holding a company back. If anything, you should be helping them get to that milestone. And I think that's why I've been able to do so well for myself because I show that, "Hey, I have the best interest for you and your company." As opposed to how much more money can I squeeze from you by holding onto you as a client. (00:38:47): I would say, agency consultant is a good way to start. Because if you as a business owner, you shouldn't have to log into, "Oh, I haven't logged into Google in three weeks to look at stuff because I'm doing payroll, I'm doing HR stuff, and I'm meeting with clients, and I'm doing sales." Start there, get it to a good place. Create that milestone of, "Hey, when we're spending 50K a month, I need to hire somebody full time to take this over." And just have that conversation with your agency and your consultant. I think more times than not, you will have a positive reaction to that. But if you don't, I would say that's a major red flag and probably someone you shouldn't be partnering with.
turns.zh: 代理是起步的好地方。即使我咨询时，老实说我非常信「向前想、向后规划」。所以如果我接这个新客户，你的终点目标是什么？如果你的终点是做到一亿刀投放规模，一个人绝不可能搞定。所以沿途设里程碑，确保我们定期检查、说什么时候该招人——无论是数据科学家、还是内部创意、还是全职替掉我。你没理由拖公司的后腿。如果有什么，你该帮他们达到那个里程碑。我觉得这就是我能做得这么好的原因——我展现出「嘿，我是为你和公司的最大利益着想的」，而不是「我还能从你这客户身上多榨多少钱」。（00:38:47）我会说，代理/顾问是起步的好方式。因为你作为老板，不该「哦，我三周没登 Google 看东西了，因为我在做工资、做 HR、在见客户、在做销售」。从那起步，做到一个好状态。设个里程碑：「嘿，当我们每月花 5 万时，我需要招个全职的来接手。」跟你的代理和顾问聊这个。多数时候你会得到正面反应。但如果没有，我会说那是个大红旗，大概不是你该合作的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so your advice is to get started on paid growth, buying an agency or a small shop consultant type person to get you started, have a conversation. And when we reach a certain scale, we're going to hire someone internally to run this for us. And then, potentially, they'll keep working with you. Potentially they'll start things in their own. Or is the assumption they'll start working with you, they'll become the owner of this thing, or is it like we may transition you out?
turns.zh: 好。所以你的建议是，起步做付费增长，找代理或小咨询顾问帮你启动，聊清楚。等到了一定规模，我们招个内部的人来管。然后他们可能继续跟你合作，也可能自己接手。还是假设他们会接手、成为这个事的主人，或者我们会把你换掉？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: That's a really good point actually. So, there have been times where a client's like, "Hey, we've reached our milestone. I want to bring someone in." That person comes in, and say, they're an expert in social media, like, "Hey, I still want you to execute on Google and Bing, because that is just not my bailiwick. I'll take over the social stuff, but we do need to talk about your fee. Maybe it does need to go down." "Completely acceptable. Let's have that discussion, make sure we're both aligned to what that should be." But yeah, there have been times where they're like, "Hey, we've reached our milestone. We got to bring someone on." But that person that they bring on is like, "Actually, I see expansion in this direction, but I can't do this. Are you willing to stay on, and help me with this? Great. If not, I'll just have to find someone else who can."
turns.zh: 这点其实很好。有过客户说「嘿，我们到里程碑了。我想招个人进来。」那人进来，比如是个社交媒体专家，说「嘿，Google 和 Bing 我还是想让你来执行，因为我搞不定。社交的我来接，但我们得聊聊你的费用，也许该降一点。」「完全接受。我们聊聊，确保对齐。」但也有过客户说「嘿，我们到里程碑了，得招人。」但招来的人说「其实我看到这个方向能扩，但我做不了这个。你愿意留下帮我做这个吗？太好了。不行的话，我得找别人。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about the team that you build over time, but later. But specifically, for this first person that you hire, what sort of person is this person? Is it like a data person? Is it a person that's just done specific performance marketing on channel? Or what do you look for ideally?
turns.zh: 我想聊聊你随着时间搭的团队，但晚点。具体来说，你招的第一个人，是个什么样的人？是数据的人？还是做过某个渠道效果营销的人？你理想中找什么样？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: I'm a big believer in... There was a book written by Nate Silver called The Signal and the Noise. Are you familiar with it?
turns.zh: 我特别信……有本书叫 Nate Silver 写的《信号与噪音》。你熟悉吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: So, Nate Silver is the guy who created.
turns.zh: Nate Silver 是创建……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: FiveThirtySeven?
turns.zh: FiveThirtyEight 的那个？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. And in the book, he basically... I'm going to use the word art, I'm going to use the word art, detailed the art of probability statistics and applied him to real world circumstances. It included case studies with baseball, which of course I loved. Elections, climate change, poker, stuff like that. And I liked that book. It's kind of dense. But the thing I liked the most about it was the title. And just changing the title ever so slightly to signal not noise. So typically, whenever I hire people, I want to hire smart people and kind of get out of their way. But the biggest thing I want to focus on is what is your thought process when it comes to data? (00:42:05): Because I can teach anyone how to do Google ads. I can teach anyone how to do Meta ads. That is not the hard part. It is the data part that is the hard part because there is so much noise going on in those accounts. They give you everything, which is great. It's great that they give you all this information, but you can have someone that's "Oh, but look at the reach, look at the frequency, look at the CPMs, look at the CPC, look at the conversion rate. Look at the cost per lead. Look at the cost per MQL. Look at this." Hold on, that's a lot of noise you just said. So what is the signal and what is the noise? And let's make sure we're focusing on the right signal versus the right noise. And that has to be a data person because there's a lot of data in these platforms.
turns.zh: 对，对。书里他 basically……我用「艺术」这个词，细致地讲了概率统计的艺术、并应用到真实场景。有棒球的案例研究，我当然爱；还有选举、气候变化、扑克之类的。我喜欢那本书。有点密。但我最喜欢的是书名。把书名稍微改一下——「信号而非噪音」。通常我招人时，想招聪明人、然后别挡他们路。但最重要的是我想聚焦：你面对数据时的思维过程是什么？（00:42:05）因为 Google 广告任何人我都能教，Meta 广告任何人我都能教。那不是难的部分。难的是数据那部分，因为这些账户里噪音太多了。它们什么都给你，这很好，给所有信息很好，但你可能会遇到有人说「哦，但你看覆盖、看频次、看 CPM、看 CPC、看转化率、看每条潜客成本、看每个 MQL 成本、看这个。」等等，你刚说了一堆噪音。所以什么是信号、什么是噪音？我们要确保聚焦在正确的信号、而不是正确的噪音上。那必须是个数据的人，因为平台里数据太多了。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. So I played baseball my whole life, but when you blow out your arm and you're as fast as a sea otter, it's not very conducive for you to continue chasing that dream. But the one thing I always liked was the stats. Even as a kid when I would watch baseball games on TV, it's like, what's this guy batting? How often is he getting on base? How many RBIs? Like, "Oh, this guy is terrible average, but he has a lot of RBIs, so that means if there's a runner on base, he may not get a hit, but he's going to get that guy in. So you want to make sure you put him in the right spot in the batting order, so on and so forth." I could talk about that for hours. But again, that could be another thing where there's a lot of data available, which one should you focus on? (00:45:16): And ultimately, what is the optimization you're going to make to the lineup or to where you place fielders on the field to ensure that we're doing the right thing and becoming as efficient and effective as possible? As far as dealing with all that data, that is just, I would say, a skill I've learned over time. Early in my career, whenever someone was like, "Oh, we have this new project. Who wants to work on it?" "I'll do it." I was always just eager like a sponge. I wanted to get in as much stuff as possible. I did SEO for a portion of my career. I did email marketing. I did affiliates. And then, eventually, I remember the first time I saw paid, because again, I was doing SEO where I was like, "Yeah, we're going to do this and we think it's going to work." But we won't know for about six months. (00:46:12): Someone showed me the paid platform. I was like, "Wait, you know this is the keyword you're bidding on. This is how many times the ad was shown, how many people clicked on it? How many... Wow, this is amazing. I need to get more into this." And that's just kind of where it started. And when I usually hire people and we go through the interview process, I make sure that they can be data focused. Really, it's just ensuring that we're focusing on that signal and not the noise. And one of the interview questions I usually ask is I throw a bunch of data points at them and then say, "Out of all that, what would you do to optimize the account?" And more times than not that they're just overwhelmed. But the people that I like are like, " Well, what's the purpose of the campaign?" (00:47:02): "The purpose of the campaign is to drive conversions." "Okay, well, I would focus here, focus on how many clicks we're getting, and how many conversions, are we targeting the right people?" Because who cares about how many impressions you're getting? Who cares about the reach? Who cares about the frequency? If the goal of the campaign is to get the conversions, that's what we should be doing. If it was awareness, it's how many people saw it. If it was a consideration, how many people were getting into the funnel and are considering us from a white paper download or a demo as the product solution that they're looking for.
turns.zh: 对。我打了一辈子棒球，但当你手臂报废、又快得像海獭，就不太适合继续追那个梦了。但我一直喜欢的是统计。即使小时候看电视上的棒球比赛，也会想「这人打击率多少？上垒频率多高？多少打点？」哦，这人平均很糟，但打点很多，意思是如果有人上垒，他可能打不中，但会把那人送回来。所以你要确保把他放在打击顺序对的位置，等等。这个我能聊几小时。但 again，这也可以是另一个「数据很多、该聚焦哪个」的情况。（00:45:16）最终，你要对打击顺序或防守站位做什么优化，才能确保做对的事、尽可能高效有效？处理所有那些数据，我会说那是我随时间学到的技能。职业生涯早期，有人一说「哦，我们有个新项目，谁想做？」「我来。」我总是像海绵一样 eager，想尽可能多塞东西进来。我职业生涯有一段做 SEO、做邮件营销、做联盟。然后我记得第一次看到付费，因为我做 SEO 时想「对，我们要做这个，觉得会行。但得大概六个月才知道。」（00:46:12）有人给我看付费平台。我说「等等，你知道你在出价的关键词是什么、广告展示了多少次、多少人点了、多少……哇，这太神了。我得深入这个。」就是这样开始的。我招人、走面试流程时，会确保他们能处理数……[截断]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great segue to the next question I wanted to ask you, which is just metrics that you love to focus on, pay attention to when you're helping people with paid ads. A lot of people think about CAC, a lot of people think about return on ad spend, LTV to CAC. I know it really depends on the goals as you said, but I guess, is there anything that you find is like, forget these metrics, these are kind of the bucket that you focus on most?
turns.zh: 那很好地引到我下一个想问的问题：你帮人做付费广告时最爱聚焦、留意的指标。很多人想 CAC、想广告支出回报 ROAS、LTV 对 CAC。我知道真的看目标，如你所说，但我猜有没有什么是你觉得「忘掉这些指标、这是我主要聚焦的那一桶」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, so for those metrics, I would say, I really hope you have a great finance partner. Shout out to Courtney and Nick the fantastic finance partners I have at Shopify. Nick's not there anymore. Sad cry emoji. But Courtney, we're able to collaborate on those things. Understand, this is the investment we're putting in, this is the expected return, this is the CAC that we can basically put a guardrail on. You have to be within. So, hopefully you have a really strong financial partner you can use for those. But as far as the stuff that I focus on, there are things that whenever we're looking at accounts, we'll kind of hyperfocus on. For example, Google will give you information about what is going on with your ad copy and how to ultimately show as often as possible. What I'm showing here is a visual of brand versus non-brand when it comes to expected click-through rate, landing page experience, and ad relevance. (00:49:08): The reason I like building reports like this is because it'll kind of show you where your hole in the ship is. If you look on the left side expected click-through rate, 75% above average. Landing page experience, 84% above average. Then you get down to ad relevance, a lot more colors than there are green, only 35% above average. So, for your brand ad copy, the clear direction you have from the data that's available to you is jump into the account and make it more relevant. That will improve your ad strength. And once you improve your ad strength, that will improve your quality score. And more times than, I think, it's a 12% increase in the number of impressions you can get if you increase from a below average to an above average for the data that's available here. And then, on the non-brand side, clear expected click-through rate, you really need to be working on. (00:50:13): And that data is also available here that you can kind of see. I put in red the one for brand, your quality score being at a nine, but your average CPC is $8. That is very interesting. It should be, the higher your CPC is, the lower your CPC should be. So that is an investigation that's like, "Hey, here's a signal, let's go do a deep dive." So there's further reports that you could look at. Looking at the ad strength again, average, excellent, good, or poor. You can see clearly on the non-brand side doing really well. They're doing really well here. Most of their ads, 46 of their ads are excellent and a bulk of their spend is going there. But if we look on the brand side, you have one ad, one ad that you could go in and just click pause on, that is a poor. And look at that CPC $7. (00:51:19): So just turning that ad off by itself, not only will... I'm a firm believer in that there's an account level quality score, not just necessarily a keyword or an ad quality score. So, just turning this one off and removing it from the account, this one ad could dramatically improve your performance. And then, Google actually tells you what you need to do to increase those strength things. So this report is ultimately powered by this one. So for your ad strength improvements, they'll tell you, "Try adding a few more unique headlines or unpinning some of the ad sets. Try including more keywords in your descriptions or your headlines." So-
turns.zh: 对，对这些指标，我会说，我真心希望你有个超棒的财务搭档。致敬 Courtney 和 Nick，我在 Shopify 的超棒财务搭档。Nick 不在了，伤心 emoji。但 Courtney，我们能就那些事协作。理解：这是我们投的，这是预期回报，这是我们能 basically 设护栏的 CAC，你得在范围内。所以希望你有个很强的财务搭档能用那些。至于我聚焦的东西，是看账户时我们会超聚焦的。比如 Google 会给你关于广告文案、以及怎么尽可能常展示的信息。我这里展示的是品牌词 vs 非品牌词在预期点击率、落地页体验、广告相关性上的对比。（00:49:08）我喜欢建这种报告的原因是，它会显示你船上的洞在哪。看左边预期点击率，高于平均 75%。落地页体验，高于平均 84%。然后到广告相关性，绿色远少于其他颜色，只有高于平均 35%。所以对你的品牌广告文案，数据给你的明确方向是：进账户、让它更相关。那会提升你的广告强度。一旦提升广告强度，就会提升质量得分。多数情况下，从低于平均提到高于平均，你能拿到的曝光数会增加 12%。然后非品牌那边，明确的预期点击率，你真的得去优化。（00:50:13）那个数据这里也能看到。我把品牌的那个标红了，质量得分是 9，但平均 CPC 是 8 刀。那……[截断]

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Including more keywords in your descriptions or your headlines. So they're actually giving you this information, but more times than not, I just feel like people are just missing this and just not taking action on it. So definitely some stuff available within the account that will help you focus on that signal versus the noise that you could be just getting from the clicks, the impressions and all those things that are available to you.
turns.zh: 比如在描述或标题里加更多关键词。所以他们其实在给你这些信息，但多数时候我觉得人们就是漏掉、不采取行动。所以账户里肯定有能帮你聚焦那个信号、而不是你从点击曝光那些东西里得到的噪音的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was amazing. For folks not watching on YouTube, you pulled up actual reports from, I think, imagine, past clients, is that what the data was from?
turns.zh: 那太棒了。没在 YouTube 上看的人，你调出来的是实际报告，我想是以前客户的，对吧，那数据来自？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so actual reports from past clients of how you evaluate, and this is Google Ads, basically.
turns.zh: 好，所以以前客户的实际报告，关于你怎么评估的，而且这个 basically 是 Google Ads。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Google Ads data. Incredible. Okay. And so within those reports, you had poor, excellent. How do you determine when something is going great? Is that something you set, like if it's above this threshold? Is that a benchmark you have, or is that Google telling you, "This is poor, or this..."
turns.zh: Google Ads 数据。难以置信。好。那些报告里你有「差、优秀」。你怎么判断一件事做得特别好？是你设的，比如超过这个阈值？还是你有个基准，还是 Google 告诉你「这是差、这是……」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, so that's Google telling you.
turns.zh: 对，那是 Google 告诉你的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: There's sometimes where you'll work really, really hard to take that poor to an average, that average to an excellent, and there's just not a whole lot you can do sometimes. It kind of is what it is. But I would argue more times than not, people are not doing those things to improve their ad strength. So just if you have the change history available in every account, in Meta, in Google, if people are doing the test to try and improve and get better, great. You have the right people working. But if not, that's a clear indication that there's definitely room for improvement.
turns.zh: 有时你拼命把「差」提到「平均」、「平均」提到「优秀」，但有时真就无能为力。它就是那样。但我会说多数时候，人们没在做那些事去提升广告强度。所以只要每个账户里有变更历史——Meta 里、Google 里——如果人们在做测试去改进、变好，太好了，你有对的人。但如果没有，那清楚说明绝对有改进空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that someone asked on Twitter is for benchmarks around any of the stuff. How do you know when your CPC is good? I guess you just look at... Do you look at Google telling you it's excellent versus poor? How do you know if your conversion rate is good? How do you know if your CAC is good?
turns.zh: Twitter 上有人问关于这些指标的基准。你怎么知道你的 CPC 好不好？我猜你看……你看 Google 告诉你「优秀 vs 差」吗？你怎么知道转化率好不好？你怎么知道 CAC 好不好？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, every industry and every company is going to be different, healthcare, lawyers, those are some of the highest cost and average CPCs I've seen. If I was to compare that industry, say to a B2B industry, it would not be very good at all. Honestly, what I would tell the user to do, every single platform has partners available, more times than not, they're kind of like salespeople. I actually really like the partners that we have at Shopify, because I do feel that they are partners. Shout out to Francisco at Google, and Sami and Alana at Meta. And Nick, and Sam, and Brian at LinkedIn, in case they all hear this. But I think they're really great partners, and they will give you that information. (00:54:44): They will actually say, "If you give me the five people you consider to be your top competitors, I will tell you if you are above or below a certain threshold." Now they can't tell you CAC because they would have to have transparency into conversions. But click-through rate, conversion rate, cost per click, things like that, they will give you that information because they will anonymize it, so you won't know who is who. If you say, "My competitor's monday.com," they won't say, "monday.com has a click-through rate of 5%." They won't tell you that. But they will tell you, "Of the competitors you gave us, and we added three more in just to say, hey, we found some people." And also to where if you only give them two, you can be like, "Oh, it's one or the other." That they'll give you that information because they want you to succeed. Because if you succeed, you spend more money on their platform. (00:55:38): So if you find out your average CPC is really high, take the actions that are in the account that tell you what you can do to lower it. But if you find out that you have a lower CPC, you're like, "Oh, great, I thought that was worse." And then you can communicate that internally to your team and say, "Hey, our average CPCs may seem high, but in reality we got with our partners, and we are on par with the industry."
turns.zh: 对，每个行业、每个公司都不同，医疗、律师，是我见过 CPC 最高的一些。如果拿那个行业比 B2B 行业，会非常糟。老实说，我会告诉用户，每个平台都有合作伙伴，多数时候他们有点像销售。我其实很喜欢我们在 Shopify 的合作伙伴，因为我真觉得他们是伙伴。致敬 Google 的 Francisco、Meta 的 Sami 和 Alana，还有 LinkedIn 的 Nick、Sam、Brian，万一他们听到。但我觉得他们是真棒的伙伴，而且会给你那个信息。（00:54:44）他们会直接说「如果你给我你认为的五个顶级竞品，我会告诉你你高于还是低于某个阈值。」他们不能告诉你 CAC，因为那需要对转化透明。但点击率、转化率、每次点击成本这些，他们会给你，因为会匿名化，你不知道谁是谁。如果你说「我竞品是 monday.com」，他们不会说「monday.com 点击率 5%」。但他们会说「你给的竞品里，我们再加三个进去」，而且如果你只给两个，你能猜「哦，非此即彼」。他们会给你信息，因为他们想你成功——你成功了，就在他们平台花更多钱。（00:55:38）所以如果你发现平均 CPC 很高，就采取账户里告诉你的、能降它的动作。但如果你发现 CPC 较低，你会「哦太好了，我以为更糟」。然后你能对内沟通「嘿，我们平均 CPC 可能显得高，但其实……[截断]

turns.zh: 懂了。所以建议是，别去求这些指标的通用基准。你可以跟你 Google、Facebook、LinkedIn 等的代表聊，他们会给你 essentially 那些数字——

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Great summary. Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 总结得好。对，对。

turns.zh: 太棒了。好，回到你刚展示的报告，那是你定制的、专门给你看「这里最该留意什么」的报告吗？还是 basically 是 Google 广告管理器的导出，然后——

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: So these are all exports, so that this is just the visualization of the data that's available. So this all data is available in every account. This is data available in the account, this is data available in the account. Now in saying that, there are more reports that we get into, like impression sharing frequency. This is something I tend to look at, that not a lot of other people do. It's not about showing as often as possible because that's what impression share tells you, and that's kind of like ego marketing. I want to be number one, I want to be there all the time. It's about showing to the right person as often as possible. (00:57:06): Instead of thinking about being on top of the page, you should think about serving the right user, which can be measured with our click share. And then Google will put us on top of the page, which we can see through our top impression share. That's what this whole visualization is here for, where I feel like a lot of people don't do this type of visualization. And this can be done by leveraging all the user data available on Google, such as demographics, locations, if any audiences, in-market audiences. Testing different bid strategies and more. (00:57:40): So the data's readily available, but it's just making the visualization a little bit more digestible. And the reason that I actually have two here to show is because this is an example of when I was working on an account back in 2023, where we started making some changes. And you can see that, clearly, our impression share, I would say was baseline. It didn't really change too much, but look at our click share going up. Because now again, we're talking more to the right people, not necessarily just everyone, generic people. Versus this campaign that was... This was the test and this was the control, and you can clearly see that we were talking to a lot of people, but no one cared about what we were talking about. So this was an easy test to call and just say, "This one's performing a lot better." And then verifying the other metrics still look good, conversion rate, number of conversions, stuff like that. This one was the clear winner, so we went in this direction.
turns.zh: 这些都是导出，只是把可用数据的可视化。所以所有数据每个账户里都有。这是账户里的数据，这是账户里的数据。话说回来，我们还有更多报告，比如曝光份额、频次。这是我常看、别人不怎么看的。它不是「尽可能常展示」，因为那是曝光份额告诉你的，有点像自我满足式营销。我想排第一、想一直都在。重点是「把对的内容尽可能常展示给对的人」。（00:57:06）与其想「霸占页面最上面」，你该想「服务对的用户」，这能用我们的点击份额衡量。然后 Google 会把我们放页面最上面，我们能通过顶部曝光份额看到。这就是整个可视化的用意，我觉得很多人不做这种可视化。这能通过利用 Google 上所有用户数据做到——人口统计、位置、任何受众、在市受众。测试不同出价策略等等。（00:57:40）所以数据现成可用，只是让可视化更易消化。我放两张图是因为这是 2023 年我做一个账户时的例子，我们开始做改动。你能看到，我们的曝光份额基本是基线，没怎么变，但看我们的点击份额在上去了。因为我们现在更多是跟对的人聊，不是泛泛的人。对比这个 campaign——这是测试组、这是对照组，你能清楚看到我们跟很多人聊了，但没人在乎我们在聊什么。所以这是个容易判定的测试，直接说……[截断]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is super cool. I love that you're showing this. And again, plug for YouTube to actually see the charts you're talking about. I see one more slide on this deck. I'm curious, what's there?
turns.zh: 这太酷了。我喜欢你展示这个。再次为 YouTube 打个广告，去看你讲的图表。这 deck 上我还有一张幻灯片。我好奇，那上面是什么？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, so this one, I'm hoping you have show notes that we can give a shout-out to somebody.
turns.zh: 对，所以这张，我希望你有 show notes 能给我们 shout-out 某个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yep. There's a website called PPC Hero. What I usually tell people is, "Terrible name, great content." The actual website used to be a little bit more cartoonish with superheroes on it, but now it's, they've refined it. But the writer there, his name's Jacob Brown. This is what he calls the true competition metric. And again, this is why I highly recommend we give people the link to the article because this does get a little dense. So what he does is that he creates four new metrics with the Auction Insights that are available. And two of those metrics are position above rate when we show, and amount of times they show and we don't. Added together, and it will show how often a competitor ranks above you in all auctions you're available for. Using this type of lens is an effective way to identify genuine threats. (00:59:56): Not that just, this data can be used to gain comprehensive insights like determining your position and impression share, but by creating a baseline that you can see how this data changes over time through different bid strategies, keyword ad copy optimizations and more. This is a very, very powerful one, because I do know a lot of people are always concerned about, "What are my competitors doing? How are they doing it? Why are they doing it?" And with all the smart bidding currently available... (01:00:25): Back in my day, it was all manual bid, so you could change the bid ever so slightly, and then be like, "Oh, now my competitor's showing above me," and this is even before Google gave us Auction Insights data. This is now available to us in the platform. Using this report will actually identify a true threat, as opposed to making an assumption based on personalization that maybe you're seeing when you Google a keyword, or using a tool like Semrush that ultimately is saying, "Oh, this person's appearing above you. Well, let's run this report and see if it's a genuine threat," as opposed to just maybe ego marketing going on.
turns.zh: 对。有个网站叫 PPC Hero。我常跟人说「名字烂，内容好」。这网站以前有点卡通、有超级英雄，现在 refined 了。但那的作者叫 Jacob Brown。他称之为「真实竞争指标」。这也是为什么我强烈建议给大家那篇文章链接，因为这有点密。他做的是用可用的 Auction Insights 建四个新指标。其中两个是「我们展示时他排上面的比率」和「他展示、我们没展示的次数」。加在一起，会显示在所有你能参与的拍卖里，竞品排你上面的频率。用这种视角能有效识别真正的威胁。（00:59:56）不只是，这数据能用来得到全面洞察，比如确定你的位置和曝光份额，但通过建一个基线，你能看这数据随不同出价策略、关键词广告文案优化等怎么变。这非常非常强，因为我知道很多人总担心「竞品在干嘛、怎么做的、为什么」。而有了现在所有智能出价……（01:00:25）我当年全是手动出价，你能微调一点点，然后「哦，现在竞品排我上面了」——这还是 Google 给我们 Auction Insights 之前。现在平台里有了。用这个报告能识别真正的威胁，而不是基于你搜关键词时看到的个性化、或者像 Semrush 那种工具说的「哦，这人排你上面」就瞎假设——跑这个报告看是不是真威胁，而不是只是自我满足式营销。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super cool. And this comes from PPC Hero, is this what you're saying?
turns.zh: 太酷了。这来自 PPC Hero，对吧，你刚说的？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. We'll definitely link to that. Are there any other tools or workflows that you find really helpful in analyzing this endless amount of data?
turns.zh: 酷。我们肯定链过去。分析这海量数据，还有别的工具或工作流你觉得特别有用吗？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Please, audience, if you are using AI in this way, let me know because a lot of this stuff I do can be a little manual and can be a little time-consuming.
