But a lot of the things, I have templates that you can load the data into, and it will just automatically give you the result from it. But yeah, right now, it is a little manual, but if there's a way to automate this through AI, please, users, contact me on LinkedIn and let me know.
turns.zh: 拜托，观众，如果你用 AI 这种方式，告诉我，因为我做的很多有点手工、有点费时。如果他们找到用 AI 自动化的办法，让我提供不敏感的信息，能弄得更干净、更易消化，告诉我。但很多事我有模板，你把数据灌进去，它自动给你结果。但 yeah，现在是手工多一点，但如果有办法用 AI 自动化，观众们，在 LinkedIn 上联系我告诉我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like a startup opportunity right there.
turns.zh: 听起来那就是个创业机会。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Okay, let's move in a slightly different direction. Attribution, what a sexy, exciting topic. So attribution, basically it's how do you assign credit to a channel and to a campaign, so that you know where growth is coming from, what's working? What's the state of attribution today? What do you find is helpful? How do people do attribution well in today's world?
turns.zh: 甜。好，换个方向。归因，多性感、多刺激的话题。归因 basically 就是你怎么给一个渠道、一个 campaign 记功，这样你知道增长从哪来、什么在起作用。今天归因的状态是什么？你觉得什么有用？现在人们怎么做好归因？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, I'm a big believer and proponent in multi-touch. I fall into the camp of more time decay. Historically, the research I've done, users tend to forget very quickly where they first found your brand. Yes, you should get credit because this is the first time they saw your brand or the first time they interacted with it, for sure, let's give you some credit for that. But definitely not the reason that they ultimately converted. Linear is fine as well, but overall, I do think attribution by itself is biased. It does not answer the question of whether the person clicking on or seeing an ad would've converted anyways, even in the absence of that ad. (01:03:24): This is why numerous companies like Netflix and eBay have done studies to get an understanding of the incrementality of paid advertising campaigns, whether that's conducting GeoX or Conversion Lift tests at important slices of the marketing channel. I know eBay was very popular when they did that experiment. I think it was like 2012, and I'll have a link for you for that as well. Where they ultimately decided to cut almost all of their brand spend, because they found that users were already going to find them through organic anyway, so they were just kind of throwing money out the window. And it was really hard for competitors to get their ads at the top of the page because their quality scores were so low.
turns.zh: 对，我是多触点归因的信徒和支持者。我属于「更多时间衰减」那一派。历史上我的研究是，用户很快会忘他们最初在哪第一次看到你品牌。对，该给你记功，因为这是他们第一次看到或互动，肯定给点功。但那绝对不是他们最终转化的原因。线性也行，但我整体觉得归因本身有偏。它回答不了这个问题：点广告或看广告的那个人，即使没有那广告，本来也会转化吗？（01:03:24）这就是为什么 Netflix、eBay 这类公司做了研究，去理解付费广告 campaign 的增量性——无论是做 GeoX 还是转化提升测试，在营销渠道的重要切片上。我知道 eBay 那实验很出名。我想是 2012 年，我也会给你链接。他们最终决定砍掉几乎全部的品牌投放，因为他们发现用户本来就通过自然渠道会找到他们，所以那基本是把钱扔出窗外。而且因为他们的质量得分太低，竞品很难把广告顶到页面最上面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so multi-touch is the way you like to think about it. Basically give credits to all of the channels that you detected the user saw your ad on, and less credit if it was further back in time.
turns.zh: 好，所以多触点是你喜欢的方式。basically 给所有你检测到用户看到你广告的渠道记功，时间越早功劳越小。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Right, yep.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then in terms of tooling, is there tools you love? Is it stuff you build in-house generally? How do people go about doing this sort of stuff?
turns.zh: 那工具方面，有你爱的工具吗？一般是内部自建？人们怎么做这类事？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, I don't know if I want to say I have been fortunate or not, but most of the companies I've worked with, like the big companies of the world, the Pinterests, the Shopifys, the IBMs of the world tend to build things in-house. So from a third-party tool, unfortunately, I don't have a whole lot of go-tos for that. So again, either that's a, I've been fortunate or I've been sheltered.
turns.zh: 对，我不知道该说我有幸还是没幸，但我待过的大公司——Pinterest、Shopify、IBM 这种——往往内部自建。所以第三方工具，不幸我没什么常去的。所以 again，要么我有幸、要么我被保护得太好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then, are there tools that you see people use, or is it just really nothing amazing out there?
turns.zh: 那有你看到人们在用的工具吗，还是真的没什么惊艳的？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, none that I've seen that's like, "Oh wow, that's amazing." I will always say, make sure you're trying to leverage the in-platform tools because the biggest thing with performance marketing is the signal you're sending the platform. Because if you are telling the platform, "Oh, I want to get more of the users that are doing this action," it's going to do a really good job of giving you that. But if that action doesn't equal business results, you're not helping yourself at the end of the day. You're giving it, again, a lot of noise instead of the right signal. So try and leverage the in-platform tools. Or if there is a tool you're using, make sure it does allow third-party integration through the Google, Meta, TikToks of the world.
turns.zh: 对，没看到什么「哦哇，太神了」的。我总说，确保你尽量用平台内的工具，因为效果营销最重要的是你发给平台的信号。因为如果你告诉平台「哦，我想拿更多做这个动作的用户」，它会做得很好。但如果那动作不等于业务结果，你最终没帮到自己。你给的又是噪音而不是对的信号。所以尽量用平台内工具。或者你用的工具，确保它允许通过 Google、Meta、TikTok 这些做第三方集成。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then let's talk about incrementality. You mentioned this idea of how do you know if the money you spent led to incremental growth that wouldn't have happened if you didn't run that ad. Is there any advice there, anything you've seen about just how to think about incrementality correctly, and not just give yourself all this credit for stuff that would've happened anyway?
turns.zh: 那聊聊增量性。你提过这个概念——怎么知道你花的钱带来了本来不会发生的增量增长？有什么建议、你见过的，关于怎么正确想增量性，而不是给自己记一大堆本来就会发生的功？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, there are many ways to judge the effectiveness of growth overall. Like some of the stuff we talked about before, brand metrics, awareness, recall, things along those lines. There are also, I know some companies look at leading indicators like visits, and clicks, or tribute, which of the efforts are linked to or perceived drivers of actions. Like leads, conversions to prospect, prospect to scale. But really the results should be coming from either that GeoX or Geo experiment or Conversion Lift. The results of those experiments should ultimately fuel the plans for what we call IAF, incrementality adjusted factor, and will allow you to be more precise and how efficient each channel is. (01:07:03): Ideally, by region, sometimes you just have a holistic of like, "This is how Meta is, this is how YouTube is." But if you don't have it by region, don't fret, it's fine, just have it by platform. And kind of like what does that look in practice? When you're running a Conversion Lift test, you intentionally do not show your ad to some users when you win an auction, and instead Google shows the next bidders' ad. This is your control group, and adds up to some opportunity costs that is estimated in terms of impression share percentage, as well as spend holdback. Spend holdback is like how much money you will not spend because of this test. (01:07:42): And all of the platforms are willing to partner with you on this, because Facebook knows this, LinkedIn knows this. All of them know that they are very visually-based creative assets that are not getting as much credit as they deserve. So if you go to any of them, if say you don't have a dedicated rep you can call, and if you ask for this, more times than not, they are willing to partner with you in saying that, if you're not spending enough, they probably will not help you with this. Because there are certain spend thresholds you do need to meet. But I would say at least start there. And also if you're not spending more than I would say 50K a month in the platform, doing this is going to be a lot more work than you're going to get result from, you're just not going to have enough signal there.
turns.zh: 对，衡量增长整体效果有很多方式。像我们之前聊的品牌指标、认知、回忆这些。也有些公司看先行指标，比如访问、点击，或归因——哪些努力关联或被认为是行动的驱动，比如潜客、潜客到转化、潜客到规模。但结果真的该来自 GeoX 或地理实验，或转化提升测试。这些实验的结果最终该驱动我们叫 IAF（增量调整系数）的计划，让你更精确、知道每个渠道多高效。（01:07:03）理想按地区，有时你只有个整体的「Meta 是这样、YouTube 是这样」。但如果没有按地区，别慌，按平台就行。实践里什么样？跑转化提升测试时，你故意在某些拍卖赢的时候不给一些用户看广告，而是 Google 展示下一个出价者的广告。这是你的对照组，会有机会成本，用曝光份额百分比和支出扣留来估算。支出扣留是因为这测试你不会花的钱。（01:07:42）所有平台都愿意配合你，因为 Facebook 知道、LinkedIn 知道，它们都知道那些视觉型创意资产没得到应得的功劳。所以你找任何一家，如果没专属代表可打电话，你要这个，多数时候他们愿意配合——如果你花得不够，他们大概不帮，因为有花费门槛。但至少从那开始。而且如果你……[截断]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So basically don't worry about running incrementality tests when you're-
turns.zh: 所以 basically 刚开始时别操心跑增量测试——

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, when you're starting out.
turns.zh: 对，刚开始时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Okay. And so basically to understand actual incrementality, every platform has a way for you to actually test it on the platform, and the team there can help you run it.
turns.zh: 懂了。好。所以 basically 要理解真正的增量性，每个平台都有办法让你在平台上实际测，那边的团队能帮你跑。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Let's go back to talking about team structure and how to build your own performance marketing team. So we talked about the first person that you hire and the advice there was someone that's very, understands how to find signal in noise. So there's that one person, and your advice there was maybe around like 50K. Was that like an actual threshold that you usually recommend, or is that just like an example?
turns.zh: 好。回到团队结构和怎么搭你自己的效果营销团队。我们聊了招的第一个人，建议是找个超懂怎么在噪音里找信号的人。就那一个人，你建议大概 5 万刀？那是你通常推荐的门槛，还是只是个例子？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Every business is slightly different. I mean, if they're well funded, 50K may not... the threshold may be higher. But yeah, everyone's different. 50K may be, like if somebody said... If you were to just say, "Hey, give me a number," I would say, "50K to start having those conversations." Because if you're at 50K, say for the month of June, great, it's going to take us three months to hire someone anyway, so at least start the conversations now.
turns.zh: 每个生意略有不同。如果资金足，5 万可能……门槛更高。但 yeah，人人不同。5 万可能，比如有人说……如果你就说「嘿，给个数」，我会说「5 万时就开始聊这个」。因为如果 5 万，比如六月，好，招个人怎么也得三个月，所以现在就开始聊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. What do the first three to five hires look like generally, that you recommend for scaling internally from its marketing?
turns.zh: 好。那前三个到五个 hires 一般长什么样，你建议从内部做大规模？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: So the first thing, like we said, someone data-driven that can get into the platforms. The next is going to be creative. Because I need those two now working hand-in-hand, making sure the creative is matching the tone and also the performance that we're trying to achieve as a business. And then third would be a dedicated data scientist, a fully dedicated person. Because they can help you with things like the incrementality testing. They can help create reports that will ultimately make everyone's lives better. They will be able to build analyses that as a generalist will not be able to do yourself. There's a saying of like, "I'm not a data scientist, but I like to play one online." Because what they do, they ultimately make us look really good. Because we're ultimately the ones reporting on the performance of it, but they were the ones that helped build that environment, and build all those things for us to succeed.
turns.zh: 首先，像我们说的，一个能进平台的数据驱动的人。下一个是创意。因为我需要这两个现在手牵手，确保创意匹配我们作为生意想达成的语气和效果。第三个是专职数据科学家，完全专职的人。因为他们能帮你做增量性测试。能建报告让大家生活更好。能做通才自己做不了的分析。有句话「我不是数据科学家，但我喜欢在网上扮演一个」。因为他们做的，最终让我们看起来很棒。因为我们是汇报表现的人，但他们是建那个环境、建所有让我们成功的东西的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then in terms of the creative person, is that like a graphic designer? Is it like a marketing person? What's the actual skill set there?
turns.zh: 那创意那个人，是平面设计师？是营销的人？实际技能是什么？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: It would be more graphic design/branding. The reason for that is because if you have a good marketing mix, you're going to have... If we keep it to a three-step funnel of awareness, consideration, purchase, you're going to need to build some brand equity in a specific direction. You're going to need to make sure you're communicating value, which now you're not being as creative, you're being more directional. And then ultimately the purchase is like, "Hey, click here, convert now." So you do want to give them the ability to still be creative. "Hey, I hired you because you have a good creative eye and you're good at what you do, but now we need to focus on getting that person to convert." So you give them a little free rein to be creative, but then you also need them to be able to execute against that creative, you need to get those users to convert.
turns.zh: 更偏平面设计/品牌。原因是如果你有好营销组合，你会……如果保持三步漏斗：认知、考虑、购买，你需要朝特定方向建一些品牌资产。你需要确保你在传达价值，这时候你不是那么创意，而是更有方向性。最终购买是「嘿，点这，现在转化」。所以你要给他们自由发挥创意的空间。「嘿，我雇你因为你创意眼光好、你擅长这个，但现在我们需要聚焦让那人转化。」所以给他们点自由发挥，但你也需要他们能执行那个创意、把那些用户转化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And they're also writing the copy, I imagine for the Google Ads.
turns.zh: 我想他们也写文案，Google Ads 的。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: I usually say that should be collaborative. The performance marketer should be able to write most of the ads, but I can't tell you how many times in my career where I've written an ad and I'm like, "This is the greatest ad ever written known to man. People will write stories about this ad, it is amazing." And it flops because I'm not the target audience, more times than not. So I think it should be collaborative, and no idea should be left on the cutting room floor because... Perfect example. I was working with ADT, the security company. We wrote the most perfect ad when Google Ads only allowed a headline and two descriptions of 35 and 35. We got every single value prop in there somehow, it was amazing. (01:12:50): And the ad that it was going against was dollar sign, zero setup fee, dollar sign, zero install fee. That ad won. It was like that is... No, how did that... It barely uses any of the characters, and it tells you almost nothing, but it won. Had more conversions, a higher click-through rate. So we took that, and we applied that with the value props, and it did better. So it should never be like, unless the idea is don't buy our product, which hopefully someone is not writing that ad copy. It shouldn't be left on the cutting room floor. Always test it. Always be willing to learn what works, what doesn't.
turns.zh: 我通常说该协作。效果营销的人该能写大多数广告，但我没法数我职业生涯里写过多少广告、然后「这是人类已知写过最伟大的广告。人们会为这广告写故事，太神了。」然后它扑街了，因为我多数时候不是目标受众。所以我觉得该协作，而且任何点子都不该被丢在剪辑室地板上，因为……完美例子。我和 ADT（安防公司）合作。Google Ads 只允许一个标题和两个 35 字的描写时，我们写了最完美的广告，把每个价值主张都塞进去了，太神了。（01:12:50）而它对打的那个广告是「$0 安装费，$0 设置费」。那个赢了。就像……不，怎么会……它几乎没用几个字，告诉你几乎什么都没有，但它赢了。更多转化、更高点击率。于是我们拿那个，配上价值主张，表现更好。所以永远不该像——除非点子是「别买我们产品」，希望没人写那种文案。不该被丢在剪辑室。永远测。永远愿意学什么行、什么不行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For this first hire, what's the title of this person, usually in your experience?
turns.zh: 这第一个 hire，这人的 title 一般是什么，你经验里？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Lately, it's been growth marketing specialist, growth marketing manager, because they're going to wear multiple hats. Like at any startup that you're at, you're going to be asked one day to, "Hey, I want you to do performance ads," and then tomorrow it's like, "Hey, I need you to help me build out this spreadsheet for a spec sheet that you have no idea what you're doing." So you're always going to wear multiple hats, so just having a general title like that to start out with. And then if that person matures into a role, you can make them more of a specialist. Or if they start showing signs of like, "Hey, I really like doing the social stuff, and we've scaled enough. Okay, let me hire a paid search person." So yeah, I always start with a general, and then as the team grows, we get more into specialties.
turns.zh: 最近是 growth marketing specialist、growth marketing manager，因为他们要戴多顶帽子。任何初创，某天让你「嘿，做效果广告」，明天「嘿，帮我把这个 spec sheet 的表格建出来，你完全不知道在干嘛」。所以你总是戴多顶帽子，所以起步用个通用 title。然后如果那人成熟成某个角色，你可以让他更专精。或者他显出「嘿，我真的喜欢做社交」，而我们也够大了，「好，我招个付费搜索的人」。所以我总从通用开始，团队长大了再更专精。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So growth marketing person, it's kind of like the broad umbrella.
turns.zh: 所以增长营销的人，是个大伞。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then are these people sitting in Google Ad Manager and Meta Ads and just like running ads manually?
turns.zh: 那这些人是坐在 Google 广告管理器和 Meta 广告里、手动跑广告吗？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: At Shopify, we call it GSD, getting shit done. I'm a firm believer in getting shit done. You should be in the account, like I mentioned earlier with that ops cadence, we have stuff we need to be doing weekly, bi-weekly, monthly. The bigger the company gets, the [inaudible 01:14:55] you wind up in more and more meetings talking about the things you want to do, and how you're going to do it and stuff like that. But keeping those people kind of sheltered away from that and focused on those things, are going to drive the best results for you, you possibly can get. (01:15:11): And that means hands-on keyboards in the Ads Manager, tweaking things. Setting up a calendar. I'm a firm believer in setting up a calendar. "We started this test on this day, that means this test will end a month from now." Put a notification, so you have a cool down period, and you report out to the org what you did, how you did it, why you did it, and then the results from it. And then, all right, what we learned from this is this, and we will be applying that to our next test, and this is how. So yeah, hands-on keyboards doing all of those things. So again, hiring those smart people, and just getting out of their way.
turns.zh: 在 Shopify 我们叫 GSD——把事搞定（getting shit done）。我坚信把事搞定。你该在账户里，像我之前说的运营节奏，我们有每周、双周、每月该做的事。公司越大，你陷进越来越多会、聊你想做什么、怎么做。（01:15:11）但让那些人避开那些、聚焦这些事，能给你尽可能好的结果。（01:15:11）意思是亲手在广告管理器里调、改东西。建个日历。我坚信建日历。「我们这天开始这测试，意味着一个月后结束。」设个提醒，有个冷却期，然后向组织汇报你做了什么、怎么做、为什么，以及结果。然后，我们学到的是这个，会应用到下个测试，这是怎么应用。所以 yeah，亲手操作做所有这些。再次，招聪明人，然后别挡他们路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. In terms of how this team grows, you mentioned when we were chatting, that you wait for someone to cry uncle, to hire more and to add to the team to kind of avoid bloat. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢。关于团队怎么成长，你之前聊过，你等有人「叫叔叔」（撑不住）才加人、避免膨胀。聊聊这个。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Unfortunately, we've seen a lot in the news lately with a lot of tech companies letting go of some really talented people, and that is, I feel like just created bloated organizations. We, every month, my current manager, Dean, created this calculator that we look at that says, "How much time are you spending in meetings?" If you have any PTO coming up, put that in there. Optimizations, reporting, stuff like that to basically add up to how many days are in the quarter? Because every quarter... Well, not every quarter, but most quarters you'll have vacation, or you'll have, say, what we call a Shopify burst, where it's we meet in real life to get shit done in real life as opposed to remotely. Put all that in there, and then what does the number equate to? Oh, we're in the red right now for these two to five people. (01:16:59): How many quarters has it been that way? Okay, it's only this quarter. This quarter, we have a summit coming up, or we have a burst coming up, or we have a lot of travel because we're meeting with partners, so on and so forth. So maybe this is an isolated thing, let's go ahead and wait till next quarter. All right, next quarter, it's red again. All right, now maybe we need to start having the conversation of, what this new hire will take over, what they will be responsible for, and how much work they'll be taking on and doing, to replace some of this red that is going on. (01:17:31): And if it equates to a full head, great, we can move forward, we've made our business case. But sometimes it doesn't. Sometimes we're just red, and we need to do a better job of making sure, "Hey, we need to step out of these meetings. These meetings are sucking out our time and we don't need to be a part of it." Or, "This launch, we don't need to be a part of. We just need to be consulted on it. We don't need to be in every single meeting every single time, or every single communication." So just making sure we're looking at the right things before we decide to hire someone and making-
turns.zh: 不幸我们最近新闻里看到很多科技公司裁掉很有才的人，我觉得那就是造了臃肿组织。我们每个月，我现在的经理 Dean 做了个计算器，我们看「你多少时间花在会上？」如果有假要休，算进去。优化、汇报这些，加起来等于季度多少天？因为每季……不是每季，但多数季度你有假期，或有我们叫 Shopify burst 的——线下见面、线下把事搞定，而不是远程。全算进去，那数字等于什么？哦，这两到五个人现在红了。（01:16:59）红了多久了？哦，就这季。这季我们有峰会、有 burst、有好多出差见伙伴，等等。所以可能孤立事件，等下季。下季，又红了。好，现在也许我们该开始聊：这新 hire 会接手什么、负责什么、会扛多少工作量，来替换一些红。（01:17:31）如果等于一个整人头，太好了，我们能推进，商业理由成立。但有时不是。有时我们就红了，需要更好地确保「嘿，我们得退出这些会。这些会吸走我们的时间，我们不需要参与。」或者「这发布我们不需要参与，只要被咨询就行。不需要每次每场会、每次沟通都在。」所以确保在决定招人前看对的东西……[截断]

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Just making sure we're looking at the right things before we decide to hire someone and making sure that we have stuff for them to do.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And red means they have more work?
turns.zh: 红意味着他们活更多？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. More days than there are in the quarter.
turns.zh: 对。比季度里的天数还多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so they basically estimate, "Here's how many days I need to do the things I've committed to for the quarter." And then it's like, "How many actual days do you have this quarter?"
turns.zh: 所以他们 basically 估算「我这一季承诺要做的事需要多少天」，然后「这一季你实际有多少天？」

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool. And so step one is, 'Okay, if you're in the red, let's cut some stuff." And then if they're still in the red and you've cut stuff, then, " Okay, we need to start hiring."
turns.zh: 太酷了。所以第一步是「好，如果你红了，我们先砍点东西」。然后如果砍了还红，「好，我们得开始招人了」。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is very cool. Is that a Shopify thing or is that something you do at your team?
turns.zh: 太酷了。那是 Shopify 的东西，还是你团队里做的？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: I've done stuff like that at other companies before, but kind of bringing it forward again, I don't want to take the credit for it. Dean was the one that brought it back up. It was like, "Oh yeah, I used to do this. I don't know why I stopped doing it." So it's definitely something I've used at other companies for sure.
turns.zh: 我在别的公司也做过类似的，但再说一遍，我不想抢功。是 Dean 又把它提回来的。就像「哦对，我以前做过这个。不知道为什么停了。」所以肯定我在别的公司用过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super cool. You mentioned this opps cadence. Is that something you can describe just what this cadence looks like of how you run?
turns.zh: 太酷了。你提过这个运营节奏。能描述一下你跑的这个节奏长什么样吗？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. So I love me a spreadsheet. So it's just a spreadsheet. And visually, I'll do my best to describe it. Let's say column A has those buckets I was talking about a finance, performance structure, keywords, so on and so forth. And then within those buckets ... Or let's call those ... Everyone loves rocks and pebbles right now, right? So that's your big rock. Your big rock is keywords. (01:19:24): Then within that you have pebbles. Keyword granularity, brand versus non-brand, search query reports, negatives, so on, so forth. And then within that we say how often we're doing it. Are we doing it weekly, bi-weekly, monthly? And then that allows us to ... If anyone in the organization's like, "Hey, how often are you guys updating ad copy?" Easy answer. "How often are you guys doing search query reports?" Easy answer, And it allows us to make sure we hold ourselves accountable to those things because a lot of times we have a lot we're doing, We're working in Google, we're working in Meta, we're working in YouTube. You could easily forget, "Oh, I didn't do that. I got to make sure I do that again." So it's a way to hold yourself accountable, but it's also a way for me as a manager to go in and kind of spot check that and make sure that they're doing the things that need to be done in the account.
turns.zh: 对。我超爱表格。就是个表格。视觉上我尽力描述。假设 A 列有我说的那些桶：财务、效果、结构、关键词等等。或者叫它们……大家都爱「大石头和小石子」对吧？那是你的大石头。你的大石头是关键词。（01:19:24）然后在里面你有石子：关键词粒度、品牌 vs 非品牌、搜索词报告、否定词等等。然后在里面我们说多久做一次：每周、双周、每月？这让我们……如果组织里任何人「嘿，你们多久更新一次广告文案？」容易答。「你们多久做搜索词报告？」容易答。而且它让我们确保对自己问责，因为很多时候我们做很多，在 Google、Meta、YouTube 里。你容易忘「哦，我没做那个。得确保再做。」所以这是对自己问责的方式，也是我作为经理进去抽查、确保他们在账户里做该做的事的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The core of this, essentially, there's a spreadsheet that everyone aligns on of here's when and how often we do certain activity to operate this performance marketing machine that you've built.
turns.zh: 这的核心，basically 有个表格，大家对齐「这些活动我们什么时候、多频繁做」，来运转你建的这个效果营销机器。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And it's both internally so that everyone knows, and then also when people ask, "Hey, when are you going to do this?" "Okay, here's the data."
turns.zh: 而且它内部人人知道，然后别人问「嘿，你什么时候做这个？」「好，数据在这。」

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. So if a cross-functional team or partner wants to know, easy answer. "We got it for you right here. Here's our whole opps cadence."
turns.zh: 对，对。所以如果一个跨职能团队或伙伴想知道，容易答。「我们这就给你。这是我们的整个运营节奏。」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of the team, something else folks told me about you is that you're very hardcore about training new people that you hire. What does people mean by that?
turns.zh: 关于团队，别人跟我说你对新招的人训练特别狠。那是什么意思？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. There's a book called ... I think it's The First 90 Days, and in it actually has a graph that shows when the person starts having impact and how many days it's been. And more times than not, it takes about ... We've all heard it. 90 days for someone to have impact. (01:21:14): I want to try and make that 45 days, if not 30. Most of the time it has to do with learning the culture, learning the people understanding, "Yes, you've done paid before at this other job, but this is how we do it here." That's where the opps cadence really comes in handy. It's like, "Here's how often we do it here. I understand maybe you did it monthly there, but we do it here biweekly. And you're saying you used to do it biweekly, we do it weekly and this is how." (01:21:47): And also giving them responsibility early on for something. For example, Kat on my team was hired 8ish months ago. She was thrown into the fire very quickly. It was like, "Hey, we have this campaign coming up called additions. Here's everything we did last additions. This is the results. These are your responsibilities, these are the expectations. Go. Go forth and conquer. As you come along. There may be something that doesn't make sense. I'm here by all means ask questions." (01:22:24): But what I've noticed is twofold. One, when you're clear in what is expected of them, like, "You are expected to do this when and you already know how to do it. Great." Or also in one-on-ones, I'll just open up the account and say, "Hey, this is how I do it. Let me show you the way I'm doing it and how quick it is for me. And you can learn, even though we're remote, I'm showing you as if you're sitting right over my shoulder or we're face to face. This is how I do it." So if you're doing something different maybe ... One plus one is two, three minus one is two, and that's fine. We both got to the same answer. But if you're doing nine times five minus two times 12 divided by 15, nope, we can simplify this." (01:23:13): So making sure that they're efficient and effective with their time, they're focusing on that signal versus that noise and giving them responsibility early on to really take ownership of something. You can see that people are a lot more quicker to pick up things and start getting that flywheel going of, "Hey, I want to have impact as soon as possible." Versus, "Oh, hey, go read this handbook week one. Week two, let me introduce you to the team. Week three." It's like slow rolling. "We can speed this up guys. We can get people up to speed and making impact a lot sooner." (01:23:52): And also don't expect them to be perfect. You can't expect people to be perfect right out the gate. " I can't remember every little thing I need to tell you, and there may be things I can learn from you." I can't tell you how many times I'm still learning from people around me. It's like, "Oh, that's great. I didn't even think of that or I haven't tried that. I should totally do that." So just know that they're not going to be perfect out of the gate, but giving them clear direction and expectations, we'll get them where they need to be.
turns.zh: 对。有本书叫……我想是《The First 90 Days》（上任头 90 天），里面有个图显示人什么时候开始有影响、过了多少天。多数时候要……我们都听过，90 天才有影响。（01:21:14）我想试着压到 45 天，最好 30。多数时候跟学文化、学人、理解「对，你以前在别的工作做过付费，但我们这这么做」有关。那就是运营节奏派上用场的地方。「这是我们这多久做一次。我理解你那可能每月做，但我们这双周。你说你以前双周，我们这每周，就这么着。」（01:21:47）而且早点给他们责任。比如我团队的 Kat，八个月前招的。很快把她扔火里。就像「嘿，我们有个叫 additions 的 campaign 要来。这是上次 additions 我们做的所有事、这是结果、这是你的责任、这是期望。去吧，去征服。过程中有什么不对的，我随时在，问。」（01:22:24）但我注意到两点。一，当你清楚期望是什么——「你被期望这时做这个、而且你已经知道怎么做。太好了。」或者一对一里，我直接打开账户说「嘿，我是这么做的。让你看我多快。你在学，即使远程，我像你坐我旁边一样演示。我是这么做的。」所以如果你做的不一样也许……一加一等于二，三减一等于二，那没问题，我们都到同一答案。但如果你做九乘五减二乘十二除以十五，不，我们能简化。（01:23:13）……[截断]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see why your team is so effective and so successful. This all makes a lot of sense. You mind if I do a rapid fire set of questions that people asked on Twitter about very specific stuff?
turns.zh: 我能理解你团队为什么这么有效、这么成功。都很有道理。你介意我来一组 Twitter 上大家问的、非常具体的问题快问快答吗？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. By all means.
turns.zh: 当然，尽管来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, ATT, there was a huge change to the way cookies and attribution and tracking worked online and it felt like paid ads kind of like, "Oh, shit. That's not going to work anymore. It's over. Facebook is dead." Clearly that hasn't happened at this point. Just what is the impact that ATT has had on paid ads and performance marketing?
turns.zh: 好，ATT（苹果应用追踪透明度）对 cookie、归因、追踪的方式有大改动，当时感觉付费广告像「哦糟，那不行了，完了。Facebook 死了。」显然到现在没发生。ATT 对付费广告和效果营销到底有什么影响？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: We were just talking about this the other day because we have ... Full transparency, we have people fully dedicated to mobile on the team, and I had reached out to Sasha who's on the team and said, "Hey, what are we doing with ATT? What are we doing scan? All those things? Because has any of our tactics really changed because of say, low opt-in rates?" And the direct answer I got from her was, "As long as we can use scan to provide attribution and measurement for iOS, we're fine." It's like, "Okay, that's very straightforward. I appreciate it." So as long as you're doing those things, you should be okay.
turns.zh: 我们几天前刚聊这个，因为我们有……坦白讲，团队里有专门做移动的人，我找了团队里的 Sasha 说「嘿，我们对 ATT 怎么做？对 scan 怎么做？所有这些？因为我们的策略真因为低 opt-in 率变了吗？」她直接回答我「只要我们能用电信 scan 给 iOS 做归因和衡量，我们就没事。」就像「好，很直接，谢了。」所以只要你在做那些事，应该没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. That's great. So basically the show goes on, things change, but people find ways to work around it. Okay. Creatives, how impactful are creative in the performance of ads generally? Is that like, "Holy shit. People are way under estimating the power of a creative." Or is it like, "Okay, it's like a fringe impact?"
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以 basically 节目继续，东西在变，但人们找到绕过的办法。好。创意，创意对广告表现一般多大影响？是「天哪，人们严重低估了创意的力量」，还是「哦，边缘影响」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Way underestimating the power of creative. The best example I can give ... Do you remember Dollar Shave Club?
turns.zh: 严重低估创意的力量。最好的例子……你记得 Dollar Shave Club 吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Their video.
turns.zh: 绝对。他们的视频。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: All right. There you go. You remember it. That was creative. Now the person buying it may have done a really good job of just targeting males, but I would argue girlfriends at the time probably would've been aware of it as well. Really good creative should be doing a really good job of telling a story. And if it does that ... Again, going back to what we talked about at the very beginning, if you get that emotion with users, whether that's pulling at the hard strings or comedy, it's going to have a lasting impact.
turns.zh: 好。你想起来了。那就是创意。当时买它的人可能很好地把目标定在男性，但我会说当时的女朋友们大概也知道了。真正好的创意该很好地讲故事。如果做到……回到我们最开始聊的，如果你跟用户建立了情绪——无论是扯心弦还是喜剧——会有持久影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Chuck on Twitter asked, "When someone steals your traffic, say in Google search results and buying up keywords around your companies, what should you do? Any advice?"
turns.zh: 好。Twitter 上 Chuck 问「有人偷你流量，比如在 Google 搜索结果里买你公司周边的关键词，你该怎么做？有建议吗？」

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. So that actually goes back to the visual that we showed and I'll pull it back up as I'm talking through it. The biggest thing is just know that anyone can do that. You can do it too, if you are ultimately concerned about it. But a lot of times competitors could be doing it on accident. And what I mean by accident is within Google, if you're bidding on keywords, Google will do what's called a close variant. If you were to do say e-commerce solution, I bet you Shopify shows up as a close variant at some point or Square or anyone like that. So they could just be mismanaging their account first and foremost. Don't give them that much credit that they're doing this maliciously or even doing it with intent. (01:27:59): And again, it will be in the show notes. If you do pull this report and you do notice that there is a clear threat that's going on here, first things first, let's make sure that they're not doing anything egregious like saying, "Lenny and Tim are better than Monday.com." (01:28:15): You cannot be, if the brand is trademarked within Google, they cannot use your name within the ad copy. Google more times than not will disallow it, but they could misspell it. I can't tell you how many times I've seen Shopify spelled with two I's because Google isn't catching it, but we can always put in a claim to say, "Hey Google, please remove this." (01:28:40): But if we do run this ...You can kind of see that the orange line here, and for those that are just listening. Orange line is rather consistent over time. There is a two week period where it dips, but it does come back up. There's another line that at the beginning of this visual, green is actually above orange. And if you look at the green one over time it almost disappears. So the reason I would say make sure you're looking at this report, and it's not just ego marketing, it could be an error. The issue could be the green one, specifically, could have been getting a close variant. They identified it, they removed it. "Oh wait, a couple of weeks later, we didn't fully remove it. Now let's remove it completely. And now they're almost gone completely." So make sure you're looking at the data and reacting to consistent competitor conquesting versus something that could just be an accident or users not knowing what they're doing.
turns.zh: 对。这其实回到我们展示的那个可视化，我边说边调出来。最大的事是知道任何人都能这么做。如果你真担心，你也能做。但很多时候竞品可能是无意中做的。我说的无意，是在 Google 里，如果你出价关键词，Google 会做叫「紧密变体」的事。如果你出价「电商解决方案」，我打赌 Shopify 某个时候会以紧密变体出现，或者 Square 或任何一家。所以他们可能首先只是账户管理不当。别给他们太多功劳，说他们恶意或故意。而且你会看到……（01:27:59）会在 show notes 里。如果你真拉这个报告、注意到这儿真有个明确威胁，第一件事，确保他们没做什么过分的，比如「Lenny 和 Tim 比 Monday.com 好」。（01:28:15）如果品牌在 Google 里是注册商标，他们不能在广告文案里用你名字。Google 多数时候会禁，但他们可能拼错。我数不清见过多少次 Shopify 被拼成两个 i，因为 Google 没抓到，但我们总能提申诉说「嘿 Google，请移除这个。」（01:28:40）但如果我们跑这个……你能看到橙线在这，只听的人，橙线随时间相当稳定。有两周期它掉下去，但又回来了。另一条线在图开头，绿线其实在橙线上面。随时间看绿线几乎消失了。所以我为什么说确保你看这个报告，而且这不只自我满足式营销，可能是个错误。问题可能 specifically 在绿线，可能拿到了紧密变体。他们识别……[截断]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And this is PPC Hero again, right? PPChero.com or whatever?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这又是 PPC Hero，对吧？ppchero.com 之类的？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool.
turns.zh: 好，酷。

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: We'll share it.
turns.zh: 我们会分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. We'll link it to it in the show notes. Okay. Last question. AI. You mentioned AI. You're looking for AI tools to help you with your workflows and analyze data. I guess is there anything you've seen AI impact in the work of paid growth and performance marketing, or is it like in the future might, other than obviously the algorithms on the platforms?
turns.zh: 对。我们会在 show notes 里链过去。好。最后一个问题。AI。你提过 AI。你在找 AI 工具帮你工作流和分析数据。我猜有没有你看到 AI 对付费增长和效果营销工作的影响，还是说除了平台算法外、未来可能有？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: I remember having this conversation a couple of months ago. AI, couldn't get away from it, right? It was everywhere, and what we were doing was leadership on know, "In all of our quarterly planning, what are we doing about AI? How are we using ai? What are we doing that's different?" (01:30:28): As always, I go to the partners and I say, "Hey, what are we doing about this?" And Francisco at Google, actually, he made a really good point. "You guys have been using AI for years now. Smart Bidding is AI. All of the recommendations within Google Ads is AI. Ad copy recommendations is AI, and that's always been in the platform, so we've always used those things." (01:30:59): So it was kind of like, let's reset the conversation of, "Hey, this has been here. We have been using it, this is how we've been using it and moving forward, these are some of the things we think we'll start doing." I do think it's having a huge impact from a content standpoint and a creative standpoint. Now, if those two kind of converge together, you have a perfect storm, right? But it is something that I keep a relative close eye on, but like I said earlier, hopefully some of your users can share more information with me. But it's not something that I would say is overly impactful yet, but I could see how it could be used maliciously if you can do API connections and things along those lines, for sure.
turns.zh: 我记得几个月前聊过这个。AI，躲不掉对吧？到处都是，我们领导层在季度规划里说「在所有季度规划里，我们对 AI 做什么？怎么用 AI？我们做什么不同的？」（01:30:28）像往常，我去找合作伙伴说「嘿，我们对这个做什么？」Google 的 Francisco 其实提了个好点。「你们用好几年 AI 了。智能出价就是 AI。Google Ads 里所有建议都是 AI。广告文案建议是 AI，那一直就在平台里，所以我们一直用那些。」（01:30:59）所以有点像重置对话「嘿，这东西一直在这。我们一直在用，这是怎么用的，往前看，这些是我们认为会开始做的。」我确实觉得它从内容角度、创意角度有很大影响。现在如果这两块合流，就是完美风暴对吧？但我保持密切关注，但像我早说的，希望你们一些用户能跟我分享更多信息。但它还不是我会说「影响超大」的东西，但我能看到如果做 API 连接之类，它确实能被恶意用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, what do you mean by that?
turns.zh: 等等，你什么意思？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Again, Google will disallow certain things, but it takes time sometimes. If the term is copyrighted in Google for ad copy, it'll disallow it immediately. But say they need to do a check, you'll see a lot of times under review or pending in the account. But you'll also see impressions potentially attached to that. It's because Google's like, "Oh, we'll serve a little bit of it, and then if it's malicious, we'll pull it back." I could see a way that somebody could automate AI to where it's always updating it to where it's like, "Oh, let's just get a little drip here, a little drip here, a little drip here." And that little drip equates to a lot, but that's something AI could help with a human doing that would just take forever and be a total waste of time.
turns.zh: again，Google 会禁某些东西，但有时要时间。如果术语在 Google 里对广告文案是版权保护的，会立刻禁。但如果他们需要检查，你会常看到账户里「审核中」或「待定」。但你也可能看到曝光可能挂在那。因为 Google 像「哦，我们先放一点，如果恶意再撤」。我能想到有人能用 AI 自动化，一直更新，「哦，就滴一点、滴一点、滴一点」。那一点滴加起来很多，但那是 AI 能帮人做、否则人要花 forever、纯浪费时间的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Just run tons of ads, just keep trying, trying, trying trying stuff. Slip through the cracks. You mentioned creative. It actually came back to question I forgot to ask. Going back to the team that you hired to run this sort of stuff, you hire this one person, growth marketer, specialist type of person, and the next hire is a creative. What's a sign that it's time to hire the creative person? Is there anything there? Is it just like, "We have budget and this is working?" Or is there anything else of, "Like, okay, this is a good time?"
turns.zh: 懂了。就是跑海量广告，一直试、试、试、试，从缝里溜过去。你提过创意。它其实回到我忘了问的问题。回到你招来跑这类事的那个人，你招这一个增长营销专家之类的人，下一个 hire 是创意。什么时候该招创意？有什么信号吗？就「我们有预算、这行得通」？还是别的「好，这是个好时机」？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, if you're using a creative agency and they're getting you everything you want and you're happy with it, then it may not make sense to hire a creative. But more times not what I've noticed from creative ... Creative independence tend to do better than an agency. The biggest difference I see is that matching the right tone, matching the right creative look and feel that you're going for is accomplished way better in-house, and also coming up with new ideas that you can test quickly and iterate on versus, "We only have so many hours with the agency this month, or we only have so much budget we can spend with them." Where if you have that person in-house fully dedicated to the product itself, you'll never run into those caps.
turns.zh: 对，如果你用创意代理、他们给你想要的一切、你满意，那可能没理由招创意。但我注意到的多数情况，创意……创意独立（内部）往往比代理做得好。最大区别是，匹配对的语气、对的创意观感，内部做得好太多；而且能想出新点子快速测试迭代，而不是「我们这月跟代理只有这么多小时、或只有这么多预算」。如果你有内部专职的人，你永远撞不到那些上限。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like if anywhere that scenario AI is going to empower that initial hire to do more creative on their own, you would think?
turns.zh: 感觉那种情况下，AI 会让第一个 hire 能自己做更多创意，你会想？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. And that's not always the best way to go. I've seen some ads in there where it's like, "Oh yeah, they're being scrappy. I see what they're doing." But to your point, maybe that's where AI kind of bridges the gap. Because I can't tell you how many times in the past it's like, Guys, we've got to be able to do retargeting, but we have no creative to do." Google has the dynamic ad builder and they've had it for I feel like years now, and that was just like, "Give us a couple of images and we will make a display ad for you that should perform because we're testing many different iterations of it." Meta is probably going to come along with something as well that it's like, "Give us a picture of your product and we'll put different backgrounds on it and test what works and what doesn't." Things along those lines.
turns.zh: 对，对。但那不总是最好的方式。我见过一些广告「哦对，他们在凑合。我懂他们在干嘛。」但如你所说，也许那正是 AI 补缺口的地方。因为我数不清过去多少次「哥们，我们得能做再营销，但没创意做」。Google 有动态广告生成器，我感觉有好几年了，就是「给我们几张图，我们给你做个展示广告，应该行，因为我们在测很多不同版本」。Meta 大概也会出类似的「给我们产品图，我们换不同背景、测什么行什么不行」。这类。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes so much sense. Timothy, we've covered so much ground. This is everything I was hoping it would be. Before we get to our very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you think would be important or valuable for listeners when they're trying to do this stuff on their own? Any other nuggets left that we haven't already covered?
turns.zh: 太有道理了。Timothy，我们覆盖太多了。这就是我希望的样子。在进入超刺激的快问快答之前，你觉得还有什么重要或有价值的、听众自己试着做时能用的？还有什么我们没覆盖的干货？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah. I said it at one point, but I'll reiterate it. I'm always forward thinking, backwards planning. Just as you're going through it, "Where do you want to be and ultimately how do you think you're going to get there?" Because say your goal is to be on all platforms. "I want to be on Pinterest, I want to be on X, I want to be on everything." "Okay, forward think. That's where you want to be. Now let's backwards plan. "What can we do right now? We can do search because that's only content and that's keywords. We can do that. All right, now we need creative, but where do we start?" And then make iterations along the way. It's just always forward think, backwards plan, and that's for anything.
turns.zh: 对。我说过一次，但再强调。我总是向前想、向后规划。就你做的过程中，「你想在哪、最终你觉得怎么到那？」比如你的目标是上所有平台。「我想在 Pinterest、在 X、在所有地方。」「好，向前想。那是你想到的。现在向后规划。我们现在能做什么？我们能做搜索，因为那只有内容和关键词。能做。好，现在我们需要创意，但从哪开始？」然后沿途迭代。就是永远向前想、向后规划，对任何事都这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are other examples of forward thinking? Because in a sense everyone will be like, "I want to be on every platform." I guess what are other things that people think about when they're like, the forward thinking is like, "Oh, we want to win Google search." Is that an example of forward thinking? What else? What else should people thinking?
turns.zh: 向前想还有什么别的例子？因为某种意义上大家都会「我想上每个平台」。我猜人们想「向前想」时还有什么，比如「哦，我们想赢 Google 搜索」？那是向前想的例子吗？还有什么？人们还该想什么？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. What are those goals you want to hit? One of the things that we look at is what emerging channels to perform in it. "So what is it going to take for us to consider this channel a performing channel that is an always on, we're we're adopting it as BAU? So that's going to take a thousand conversions a month at this much spend with this much lift associated with it. So okay, we know what that looks like, so we're going to backwards plan where we're going to start. We're going to start with this one ad creative. "Okay, that works. Then we're going to go to this next ..." Because within each platform, they all have multiple types of ad units You can use. Say in LinkedIn, there's feed, there's conversation, there's video, there's carousel. So it's what are the milestones along the way that you're going to do to ultimately get it from testing emerging channel to perform them? So that would be an example of something more micro than macro.
turns.zh: 对，没错。那些你想达成的目标是什么？我们看的一件事是有哪些新兴渠道值得做。「所以我们要把一个渠道当成常态化、永远在线的表现渠道，需要什么？」那需要每月在这个花费下、这个提升下、一千次转化。好，我们知道那长什么样，所以我们向后规划从哪开始。我们从这一条广告创意开始。「好，行。然后我们去下一个……」因为每个平台里都有多种广告单元。比如 LinkedIn 有信息流、对话、视频、轮播。所以沿途的里程碑是什么，最终把它从测试新兴渠道变成表现渠道？那是比宏观更微观的例子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Well, with that, we reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 懂了。好，说到这，我们到了超刺激的快问快答。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Oh yeah.
turns.zh: 哦耶。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题。你最常推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: Daily Stoic by far. A book I read every day. Quick excerpt of what you can do from a stoic philosophy standpoint. Great By Choice is another good one. And Deep Work.
turns.zh: 《每日斯多葛》（Daily Stoic）绝对是。我每天读的书。从斯多葛哲学角度你能做什么的短摘。还有《Great By Choice》（选择卓越）。以及《深度工作》（Deep Work）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最近喜欢、真的享受的电影或剧集？

turns.speaker: Timothy Davis
turns.en: X-Men '97. Thoroughly enjoyed that. But that may be a lot of nostalgia. I actually never watched RRR when it first came out. Highly recommend that.
